units.la: ISCIPLINA Ecclesiastica, quàm necessarium & efficax medium sit, ad promovendam Ecclesiæ ædificationem, ad scandala præbentes refrænandos, ad Errores, Hæreses, Schismata, Ecclesiæ Dei exitiosa mala eliminanda; & ad confirmandam pacem, concordiam, ac unanimitatem nullus non videt. Satanas tamen ille mille fraudum artifex, ab omni ævo, omnem in eo navavit operam, ut tolleretur vel corrumperetur hoc suavissimum Iesu Christi institutum. Hanc ob causam in cunis vagiente Ecclesiâ, Imperatores Ethnicos excitavit ad tollendum Ecclesiæ potestatem, ut testatur Origenes contra Celsum. Sed quum hæc via minùs prospera fuit Diabolo, ad eam corrumpendam, extirpandam, aliam viam ingreditur, in qua per fraudes sub Papatu voti compos factus erat. At cùm Deo illi Sancto, misereri suæ dilectæ Ecclesiæ ex suo beneplacito visum fuit, hoc ei cœlitus denunciavit: Evigila, Evigila, indue robur tuum ô Sion: indue vestes ornatus tui, ô captiva filia Sionis, Esa. 52. 1. 2. Et surge, luce, quandoquidem advenit lux tua, & gloria Iehovæ super te orta est, Esa. 60. 1. Evigilate ergo omnes, quibuscunque Ecclesia Christi est chara, excitemini qui diligitis Christum; ne moremini qui statis ad ostium. Nam unanimiter signo dato concurrunt malevoli ad eam comprimendam, & dicunt: disrumdisfrumpamus & proiiciamus à nobis densos funes istorum; Sed ridet Dominus, subsanat eos. Tunc alloquitur eos in irâ suâ, & in astu ira sua perturbabit eos, & confringet istos virgâ ferreâ, ut vas figulinum dissipabit eos, Ps.2. ¥.3.4 5.9.
units.tr: Discipline in the Church, how necessary and effective a means it is for promoting the building up of the Church, for restraining offences given by scandalous persons, for eliminating errors, heresies and schisms, the deadly evils of the Church of God, and for confirming peace, concord and unanimity, no one fails to see. Yet that Satan, the artificer of a thousand frauds, has from the beginning spent every effort to remove or corrupt this most sweet institution of Jesus Christ. For this reason, while the Church was still a babe in the cradle, he stirred up heathen emperors to remove the power of the Church, as Origen bears witness against Celsus. But when this way proved less successful for the Devil, he turned to another way of corrupting and uprooting it, and under the Papacy he succeeded in his aim through deceit. But it seemed good to that holy God, from his own good pleasure, to have mercy on his beloved Church, and he proclaimed this from heaven: Awake, awake, put on your strength, O Zion; put on the garments of your beauty, O captive daughter of Zion, Isa. 52:1, 2. Arise, shine, for your light has come, and the glory of Jehovah has risen upon you, Isa. 60:1. Awake then, all of you to whom the Church of Christ is dear; rouse yourselves, you who love Christ; do not delay, you who stand at the door. For the malicious gather together with one accord at the signal to crush it, and they say: Let us break their bonds asunder and cast away their cords from us. But the Lord laughs, he holds them in derision. Then he speaks to them in his wrath, and in his anger he will terrify them, and he will break them with a rod of iron, and dash them to pieces like a potter's vessel, Ps. 2:3, 4, 5, 9.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Mihi ergo nemo jure vitio vertere potest, si disciplinæ hujus Ecclesiasticæ posteriorem partem, quæ Excommunicatione constat (quam multi tollere pertendunt, vel penitus nullum dari asserunt.) (postquam Tigvri Helvetiorvm de priori hujus Disciplinæ parte egi) probaturus contendam. Potestas & Autoritas necessaria est ad Ecclesiæ puritatem conservandam; sed non est nostra potestas coactiva, qualis est Magistratus politici: Verùm jus intime disponedi de iis quæ spectant ad Ecclesię regimen. Quòd autem sit in Ecclesia aliqua potestas vel hinc maximè probatur. (1.) Quia est Societas, Societas autem sine regimine diu stare non potest: nec meretur nomen Societatis, si exulet ab ea omne regimen. Quis enim credere potest, voluisse Christum societatem aliquam distinctam instituere, necessaria tamen ad illam societatem conservandam noluisse concedere. (2.) Quia concessæ sunt huic societati Claves ad aperiendum & claudendum, Matt. 16. 19.& potestas ligandi & solvendi, Matt. 16. 19. 20. & 18. 19. ligare autem & solvere authoritativam denotat potestatem, Gen. 40. 3. & 42. 16. 19. 24. Num. 15.34. Lev. 24. 12. 2. Reg. 17. 4. Esa. 41. 17. Ier. 40. 1. Ezech. 3. 29. Num.11.28. Psal. 105. 20. & 111. 20. & 146. 7. Iob. 12. 18. Matt. 22.13. Act.21.11. & 24. 27. Ioh. 18. 12. Sic & potestatem peccata remittendi & retinendi, Ioh. 20. 21. 22. 23. jam autem nullus non scit Clavium insigne esse, potestatem & autoritatem. (3.) Quia præscriptæ sunt regulæ, secundùm quas exercenda est hæc disciplina, quare (si nulla esset potestas Ecclesiæ:) præscribere voluerit Spiritus Sanctus modum illam potestatem exercendi ? Non entis enim nulla sunt attributa, ut docent Scholæ. Ejusmodi autem regulas dari, nullus potest negare, qui S. Pauli ad Timotheum & Titum Epistolas semel lustraverit. In his enim duabus Epistolis, quasi in vivâ tabulâ habemus depictum Ecclesiæ regimen, ut inquit Calvinus, in dedicatoria Epistola ad Dom. Somerset. commentariis suis ad Epistolas Pauli ad Timotheum præfixa. (4.) Quia expressa Scripturæ testimonia produnt, 2. Cor. 10. 8. Nam si amplius etiam quippiam glorior περὶ τῆς ἐξουσίας ἐξουσίας ἡμῶν, de potestate nostra, quam dedit Dominus nobis ad ædificationem, ac non ad destructionem vestri, & cap. 12. 10. utrobique habetur in Textu Originali ἐξουσίας, quę autoritativam demonstrat potestatem.
units.tr: No one, therefore, can rightly find fault with me if, having already treated the earlier part of this ecclesiastical discipline at Zurich in Switzerland, I now undertake to prove and maintain its latter part, which consists in excommunication (a part that many strive to abolish, or altogether deny that it exists). Power and authority are necessary for preserving the purity of the Church; but it is not a coercive power, such as that of the civil magistrate, but a right to dispose inwardly of matters that concern the government of the Church. That there is some power in the Church is proved especially by the following. (1.) Because it is a society, and a society cannot long stand without government; nor does it deserve the name of society if all government is absent from it. For who can believe that Christ wished to establish a distinct society, yet was unwilling to grant what is necessary for keeping that society in being? (2.) Because the keys to open and shut were granted to this society, Matt. 16:19, and the power of binding and loosing, Matt. 16:19, 20; 18:19. But to bind and to loose denote an authoritative power, Gen. 40:3; 42:16, 19, 24; Num. 15:34; Lev. 24:12; 2 Kings 17:4; Isa. 41:17; Jer. 40:1; Ezek. 3:29; Num. 11:28; Ps. 105:20; 111:20; 146:7; Job 12:18; Matt. 22:13; Acts 21:11; 24:27; John 18:12. So too the power of remitting and retaining sins, John 20:21, 22, 23. Now everyone knows that the mark of the keys is power and authority. (3.) Because rules have been prescribed according to which this discipline is to be exercised. Why, then (if there were no power in the Church), would the Holy Spirit have wished to prescribe the manner of exercising that power? For non-entities have no attributes, as the schools teach. That such rules have been given no one can deny who has once carefully read through St Paul's epistles to Timothy and Titus. For in these two epistles we have, as in a living picture, the government of the Church set forth, as Calvin says in the dedicatory letter to Lord Somerset prefixed to his commentaries on Paul's epistle to Timothy. (4.) Because express testimonies of Scripture declare it, 2 Cor. 10:8: For even if I should boast somewhat more of our authority, which the Lord gave us for building up and not for tearing you down, and ch. 12:10. In both places the original text has [ἐξουσίας], which denotes an authoritative power.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Hæc disciplina, quæ Excommunicatione constat, est Censura Ecclesiastica, quâ legitimâ causæ cognitione, & conscientia (si fit opus) in Nomine & Autoritate Dei ab Ecclesia quispiam propter scandali enormitatem, quod dedit, à communione fidelium excluditur, tantisper dum ex ipsius testata resipiscentia, quoad ejus fieri debet ac potest, toti Ecclesiæ conscię constiterit, cum Deo esse reconciliatum. Ad hujus disciplinæ moderationem requiritur (1) ut legitima causæ adsit cognitio. (2.) Iustis de causis exerceatur. Nam in justa excommunicatione ברכה benedictio est, Gen. 12. 4. Ps. 109. 28. Matt. 5. 11. (3.) ut sit ex præscripto Verbi Dei. (4.) In timore & tremore Domini Iesu Christi, invocato etiam Dei nomine, quia non suum, sed Dei מלאכה negotium curant, cum potestate Domini, 1. Cor. 5. 4. 6. cum spiritu mansuetudinis, summa cum clementia & charitate, Gal. 6. 1. Non enim debet esse brutum fulmen, aut fulgur è pelvi, ut habetur in proverbio; non etiam inane terriculamentum. Quia quod iniquè agitur in terris, in cœlis ratum esse potest minimè. Requiritur etiam illud, quod Augustinus, lib. 2. cap. 1. contra Parmenium, & contra Donatistas, cap. 1. lib. 3. disputat: Ne, vel, privati homines, si viderint minùs diligenter à Seniorum concilio navos corrigi, decisionem & secessionem ab Ecclesia faciant: aut Pastores, si ex animi voto, omnia repurgari nequeunt: Ideo abiiciant Ministerium, vel, inusitatâ asperitate totam Ecclesiam perturbent. Quisquis ergo, quod potest arguendo corrigit: vel quod corrigere non potest, salvo pacis vinculo excludit: vel, quod salvo pacis vinculo excludere non potest, æquitate importat, firmitate supportat, quia omnis pia ratio, & motus disciplina Ecclesiastica in Spiritus unitate in vinculo pacis, intueri semper debet.
units.tr: This discipline, which consists in excommunication, is an ecclesiastical censure, by which someone, after a lawful inquiry into the cause and (if need be) with a clear conscience, is excluded in the name and authority of God by the Church from the fellowship of the faithful, on account of the gravity of the scandal he has given, until by his attested repentance it has been established to the whole conscientious Church, so far as it ought and can be, that he has been reconciled to God. For the right moderation of this discipline the following are required: (1) that there be a lawful cause and knowledge of it; (2) that it be exercised for just reasons, for in a just excommunication there is [ברכה, benedictio] a blessing, Gen. 12:4; Ps. 109:28; Matt. 5:11; (3) that it be according to the prescription of the Word of God; (4) that it be done in the fear and trembling of the Lord Jesus Christ, with the name of God also invoked, because they attend to not their own, but God's [מלאכה, negotium] business, with the power of the Lord, 1 Cor. 5:4, 6; and with a spirit of gentleness, with the greatest kindness and love, Gal. 6:1. For it ought not to be a blind thunderbolt or a lightning bolt out of a basin, as the proverb has it, nor an empty scare-tactic either. For what is wrongly done on earth can by no means be ratified in heaven. Also required is that which Augustine argues in book 2, chapter 1, against Parmenian, and against the Donatists, book 3, chapter 1: Lest private persons, if they see that the offenders are not corrected diligently enough by the council of elders, make a separation and withdraw from the Church; or the ministers, if all things cannot be purged according to the desire of their hearts, therefore cast down the ministry, or disturb the whole Church with unusual harshness. Whoever therefore corrects by reasoning what he can correct, or, what he cannot correct, excludes while the bond of peace is preserved, or, what he cannot exclude while the bond of peace is preserved, bears with equanimity and supports with firmness; because every pious reason and motive of ecclesiastical discipline ought always to look to unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.

units.la: Hanc excommunicationem explicabimus (1) A Proprietate 2. Quòd semper in Ecclesia ab ipso mundi exordio censura Ecclesiastica in usu fuit, quâ non tantùm Ecclesia in genere à manifestè profanis hominibus sejuncta fuit: (ut olim ante diluvium Filii Dei h. e. pii ex Sethi posteris oriundi, à filiis hominum, h. e. Impiis ex Caini familia oriundis, Gen. 4. 20. 21. 25.) Sed etiam qui male & illegaliter sese gerebant, ex albo Ecclesiæ sunt ejecti, ex consortio Dei exclusi, ut nostri Protoplastæ ex eleganti horto illo Paradisi, ad miserias & lacrymas, ad labores & sudores, emissi, ejecti, & expulsi sunt, propter illegale factum, Gen.3.23.24. ויְשַׁלְּחֵהוּ יְהוָה אֱלֹהִים מִגַּן עֵדֶן sic Cainum propter occisionem Fratris sui Abelis, Genes. 4. 11. ועתה ארור אתה מן האדמה quem quum ob fratricidium pronunciat Dominus maledictum, addita perpetui à sua facie exilii pœna, simul ab externo cultu prohibet: ut rectè Augustinus dicat, lib. 15. de Civ. Dei, cap. 1. Ab eo tempore duas civitates cœpisse, unam Dei, quæ est Ecclesia, cujus peculiares sunt ritus sacri promissionibus adjuncti & extra quam non est salus: alteram vero hujus seculi, ex qua exeat oportet quisquis non vult perire. Adulti quoque qui circumcisionem neglexerunt, aut à Parentibus neglectam approbarunt, è Sanctorum consortio ex Dei mandato excisi sunt, Gen 17. 10. 11. & lepræ & aliarum segregandarum ritus, Presbyterio Synagogico præscripti sunt, Ier. 12. 2. 3. Num. 5. 2. & illis qui tetigerunt rem aliquam immundam in congregationem venire illicitum erat, Ier. 5. 2. 3. sicut mulieribus quarum dies purgationis non erant impleti, Ier. 22. 2. 3. 4. Num. 9. 6. 10. 2. Chron. 26. 20. 21. Christus quoque hunc ordinem ex Ecclesia Iudaica ad nos transtulit, & translatum expresse constituit, Matt. 16. 19. Paulus Corinthi, tum aliis in locis observandum præcipit, 1. Cor. 5. 11. 12. Titus etiam jubetur post unam atque alteram admonitionem hominem hæreticum repellere, Tit. 3. 10. Vbi hæc sunt notanda (1) Hominem hunc esse admonitum semel atque iterum, juxta normam Christi, Matth. 18. 18, propterea juxta illam repellendum esse. (2.) Admonitionem esse publicam & ministerialem. (3.) Hominem hunc hæreticum, eoque Ecclesiasticè notandum. (4.) Hoc ultimum esse remedium, quod aliud longè denotat, quàm illud, cap. 11. 15. Arguecum omni imperio, aut quàm illud cap. 1. 13. eos redarguito pracisè. Ex quibus liquet magnum fuisse excommunicationis usum à jacto mundi fundamento, ad hæc usque tempora, in Ecclesia. Imò apud ipsos Ethnicos in usu fuisse, patet, ex Cæsare, lib. 6. de Bell. Gall. ubi ait: Si quis aut privatus, aut populus Druydarum decreto non stetit sacrificiis interdicunt: hac pœna apud eos (Gallos) est gravissima: quibus ita est interdictum, ii numero impiorum ac sceleratorum habentur: ab iis omnes decedunt, aditum eorum sermonemq; defugiunt, ne quid ex contagione incommodi accipiant: neque iis petentibus jus redditur, neque honos ullus communicatur. Iosephus, lib. 2. de bell. Iudaico cap. 7. Essenos quoque excommunicatione usos esse docet, cum dicit, depellebant ex congregatione in peccatis deprehensos. 2. Quod sit ultio formidabilis Io. 9. 22. & 14. 42. seu gravissima poena, 2. Cor. 10. 6. Et paratu habendo quo vindicemus omnem contumaciam, postquam impleta fuerit vestra obedientia. Sunt qui haec de corporalibus poenis accipiunt, quibus Apostoli contumaces aut impios vindicabant: quemadmodum Petrus Ananiam & Saphiram morte, Paulus Elimam magum caecitate percussit, Act. 5. 5. & 13. 11. Sed haec, hic intelligi non possunt, quia haec extraordinaria erant, quae ad fidem & obedientiam procurandam edi solent: haec autem potestas, de qua hic loquitur Apostolus, tunc erat exercenda, quando impleta esset obedientia. 1. Quod non ad destructionem Ecclesiae sit exercenda sed ad aedificationem, ergo non praecipitanter, ergo non temere: Cum dolore enim amputatur etiam quae putruit pars corporis, & diu tractatur, si potest sanari medicamentis: si non potest, tunc a medico bono abscinditur, ut inquit Ambrosius. Offic. lib. 2. cap. 27.
units.tr: We will explain this excommunication as follows. (1) From its property. 2. From the beginning of the world the Church has always used ecclesiastical censure, by which the Church in general was not only set apart from openly profane people. (So before the flood the Sons of God, that is the pious descended from the posterity of Seth, were separated from the sons of men, that is the impious descended from the family of Cain, Gen. 4:20, 21, 25.) But also those who conducted themselves badly and unlawfully were cast off from the register of the Church and excluded from fellowship with God. Thus our first parents were sent out, cast forth and driven from that pleasant garden of Paradise, into miseries and tears, labours and sweat, because of their unlawful deed, Gen. 3:23, 24: [וַיְשַׁלְּחֵהוּ יְהוָה אֱלֹהִים מִגַּן עֵדֶן] "and the LORD God sent him forth from the garden of Eden." So also Cain, because of the murder of his brother Abel, Gen. 4:11: [וְעַתָּה אָרוּר אַתָּה מִן הָאֲדָמָה] "and now art thou cursed from the ground." When the Lord pronounced him cursed for fratricide, adding the penalty of perpetual exile from his presence, he at the same time forbade him external worship. Augustine rightly says in book 15 of the City of God, chapter 1: From that time there began to be two cities, one of God, which is the Church, whose peculiar rites are sacred and joined to the promises, and outside which there is no salvation; the other of this age, from which whoever does not wish to perish must go out. Adults also who neglected circumcision, or approved its neglect by their parents, were cut off from the fellowship of the saints by God's command, Gen. 17:10, 11. The rites of the leper and of the other persons to be set apart were prescribed by the synagogue elders, Jer. 12:2, 3; Num. 5:2. It was unlawful for those who had touched some unclean thing to come into the congregation, Jer. 5:2, 3, just as it was for women whose days of purification were not yet complete, Jer. 22:2, 3, 4; Num. 9:6, 10; 2 Chron. 26:20, 21. Christ too transferred this order from the Jewish Church to us, and expressly established it as transferred, Matt. 16:19. Paul ordered it to be observed at Corinth and in other places, 1 Cor. 5:11, 12. Titus also is commanded to reject a heretical man after one or two admonitions, Tit. 3:10. Here the following points are to be noted: (1) This man has been admonished once and again, according to the rule of Christ, Matt. 18:18, and therefore he is to be rejected according to that rule. (2) The admonition is public and ministerial. (3) This man is heretical, and therefore to be marked ecclesiastically. (4) This last is a remedy, which denotes something quite different from that in chapter 1:13, rebuke them sharply, or from that in chapter 2:15, reprove with all authority. From these things it is clear that excommunication has been greatly used in the Church from the founding of the world until these times. That it was even in use among the Gentiles themselves is evident from Caesar, book 6 of the Gallic War, where he says: If anyone, whether a private person or a people, does not abide by the decree of the Druids, they forbid him the sacrifices. Among the Gauls this is the most severe penalty. Those on whom this prohibition is laid are reckoned among the number of the impious and wicked. All avoid them, shun their approach and their conversation, lest they suffer some harm from contagion. Justice is not done to them when they ask for it, and no honour is granted to them. Josephus, in book 2 of the Jewish War, chapter 7, teaches that the Essenes also used excommunication, when he says that they expelled from the congregation those detected in sins. 2. Excommunication is a formidable vengeance, John 9:22 and 14:42, or the most severe punishment, 2 Cor. 10:6: And being ready to avenge all disobedience, when your obedience shall be fulfilled. Some take these words to refer to the bodily punishments with which the Apostles punished the contumacious or impious: as Peter struck Ananias and Sapphira with death, and Paul struck the magician Elymas with blindness, Acts 5:5 and 13:11. But these cannot be understood here, because those were extraordinary acts, usually performed to procure faith and obedience. The power of which the Apostle speaks here, however, was to be exercised when obedience had been fulfilled. 1. It is not to be exercised for the destruction of the Church but for its edification, and therefore not rashly, and therefore not carelessly: For with pain even a part of the body that has rotted is cut away, and is treated for a long time if it can be healed by medicines; if it cannot, then it is cut off by a good physician, as Ambrose says, De Officiis, book 2, chapter 27.

units.la: 2. A modo excommunicationis, Modum autem explicabimus. (1.) A causa efficiente, Ecclesia, non Magistratu politico, non enim Christus Dominus hoc regimen commisit Magistratui qua tali, Magistratui enim qua tali essent datae Claves regni coelorum. Hoc autem quam falsum sit, patet. Claves enim regni coelorum ad bonum Ecclesiae spirituale promovendum datae sunt, at potestas politica omnia agit politice, eo scilicet modo, quo se posse facilius & felicius fines politicos sibi propositos assequi judicat: Non etiam a solo pastore, seu verbi ministro; siquidem non est penes unum quempiam, 1. Cor. 5. 4. sive Episcopum, sive ab Episcopo delegatum, nedum Pontificem Romanum: sed penes Pastores, quos peculiariter Apostolus Gubernatores vocat, 1. Cor. 12. 18. & Praesbyterium Collegium Seniorum canonice & legitime electorum, 1. Tim. 4. 14. quos Christus Dominus nomine Ecclesiae designat, & eorum coetum. Toto enim Christianorum coetu conscio & consentiente quantum fieri potest, debet exerceri & usurpari. Ergo fallitur Erastus qui nomen Ecclesiæ, de uno solo sumi pertendit: Subscribunt huic nostrę sententię omnes quotquot Lexica, sive Hebraica in vocibus הקהל & עדה : sive Græca, in vocibus συναγωγὴ & ἐκκλησία ; sive Latina, in voce Ecclesia scripsere: Nec ullum locum potest Erastus afferre, sive ex V. T. sive ex N. T. ex quo nobis ostendere posset Ecclesiam ita sumi debere.
units.tr: 2. Concerning the manner of excommunication, we shall now explain that manner. (1.) As to the efficient cause, it is the Church, not the civil magistrate. For Christ the Lord did not commit this government to the magistrate as such, since the keys of the kingdom of heaven were given to the magistrate as such. How false this is becomes plain. The keys of the kingdom of heaven were given to advance the spiritual good of the Church, whereas civil power does everything in a civil way, namely in the way it judges it can more easily and successfully attain the civil ends it has set for itself. Nor does the power lie with the minister of the Word alone, whether a bishop or one delegated by a bishop, much less with the Roman Pontiff. It lies with the ministers, whom the Apostle calls by the special name of governors (1 Cor. 12:28), and with the presbytery, the college of elders canonically and lawfully elected (1 Tim. 4:14). Christ the Lord designates these by the name of the Church, and their assembly. The power is to be exercised and used with the whole assembly of Christians knowing and consenting, as far as this can be done. So Erastus is wrong when he insists that the name Church is taken of one person alone. All lexicons agree with our view, whether Hebrew, under the words [הקהל] and [עדה]; Greek, under [συναγωγὴ] and [ἐκκλησία]; or Latin, under the word Church. Nor can Erastus bring forward any passage, from the Old or the New Testament, from which he could show us that the Church must be understood in this way.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: β. A causa impulsiva, seu potenter incitante, movente, flectente, persuadente, quæ est præscriptum Iesu, Matt. 18. 15. 16. 17. Si peccaverit in te frater tuus, ito, & argue &c. si te non audiverit assume unum aut duos: & si eos neglexerit dic Ecclesiæ: quod si Ecclesiam audire neglexerit, sit tibi velut Ethnicus & Publicanus quispiam. Nota 1. hic loqui, Christum de scandalis ac Ecclesiasticis offensis, cùm dicit V. 15. Ἐὰν ὁ ἁμαρτήσῃ εἰς σὲ ὁ ἀδελφός σου, & non de injuriis civilibus quâ talibus. (1.) quia Christum Dominum in priori parte hujus capitis, locutum fuisse de scandalis extra omnem dubitationis aleam est, scandalum autem longè differt ab injuria: nam omninò ἀδικήματα, quibus unus ab altero læditur, præter jus & æquum dicto vel facto, in bonis & facultatibus suis, & ὕβρεις, quibus læditur aliter, sive in se, sive in existimatione differunt. Fateor, ἀδικήματα & ὕβρεις sunt initia scandalorum, id tamen perpetuum non est; & tunc quoque quum id accidit, ista sunt distinguenda, ut diversa, cùm posterius à priori oriatur. (2) Quia Christus Dominus docet scandala inter malorum maxima referenda esse. Quis ergo credit Christum voluisse methodum ad minima mala curanda, posthabitis his maximis præscribere. Falso ergo obtendit Erastus, quoad offensas attinet quòd sunt privatæ injuriæ, non scandala, quâ talia in societate Ecclesiastica, quod vel ex sequentibus patet. (1.) Q. scopus immediatus Christi Domini in hâc describenda ratione, non esset æterna peccatoris salus; sed saltem civilis reconciliatio & pax, quod falsum. (2.) Quia præcipuus læsi scopus esset quid ad seipsum spectans, ut haberet nempe fratrem sibi amicum; non autem ut fratrem Deo lucraretur. (3.) Quia acquiescere teneretur tum læsus, quando adversarius iram deponit, licet nondum resipiscat. (4.) Q. Etiam cum Ethnicis debemus in pace vivere, Rom. 12. 18. Heb. 12. 14. (5.) Q. Illud ἐλέγξον αὐτὸν evincit contrarium, ἐλέγχω enim significat, arguo, reprehendo, convinco, peccati arguo, 1. Tim. 5. 20. Tit. 1. 13. Nunquam pacem & reconciliationem peto. (6.) Q. Multa secum trahit absurda. Nam ν. illud ἐαν δὲ, cohaesionem nullam denotabit. 2. Ecclesia multitudinem aliquam confusam denotabit. 3. Sequentia v. 18. connexionem cum his nullam habebunt, contra istorum verborum vim amen dico vobis, vide Matth. 5. 26. & 6. 2. & 8. 10. & 10. 15. & 11. 11. & 18. 3. & 19. 23. Marc. 10. 15. & 12. 43. & 13. 30. Luc 12. 37. 7. Arguere, erit reconciliationem petere. π. Peccare in te, idem erit, quod personalem injuriam ferre.
units.tr: β. As to the impelling cause, that is, what powerfully stirs, moves, bends and persuades, it is the command of Jesus, Matt. 18:15–17: "If your brother sins against you, go and reprove him, etc. If he does not hear you, take with you one or two. And if he neglects them, tell it to the Church; but if he neglects to hear the Church, let him be to you as a heathen and a tax collector." Note first that Christ here speaks of scandals and ecclesiastical offences, when he says in verse 15, "If your brother sins against you" [Ἐὰν ὁ ἁμαρτήσῃ εἰς σὲ ὁ ἀδελφός σου], and not of civil injuries as such. (1.) Because it is beyond all doubt that in the first part of this chapter Christ spoke of scandals, and a scandal differs far from an injury. For wrongs [ἀδικήματα], by which one is harmed by another in goods and property through word or deed contrary to right and justice, and insults [ὕβρεις], by which one is harmed otherwise, either in person or in reputation, are altogether different things. I grant that wrongs and insults are the beginnings of scandals, but this is not always so; and even when it does happen, they must still be distinguished as different things, since the latter arises from the former. (2.) Because Christ the Lord teaches that scandals are to be counted among the greatest evils. Who then would believe that Christ wished to prescribe a method for curing the smallest evils and pass over these greatest ones? So Erastus wrongly objects, as far as offences are concerned, that they are private injuries and not scandals as such in ecclesiastical society. This is plain even from what follows. (1.) Because the immediate aim of Christ the Lord in describing this procedure would not be the eternal salvation of the sinner, but at least civil reconciliation and peace, which is false. (2.) Because the chief aim of the injured party would concern himself, namely that he might have his brother as a friend to himself, and not that he might win his brother for God. (3.) Because the injured party would be bound to rest content once the adversary laid down his anger, even if he had not yet repented. (4.) Because we ought to live in peace even with heathens (Rom. 12:18; Heb. 12:14). (5.) Because the words "reprove him" [ἐλέγξον αὐτὸν] prove the contrary. For [ἐλέγχω] means to argue, rebuke, convict, to reprove of sin (1 Tim. 5:20; Titus 1:13), and never to seek peace and reconciliation. (6.) Because it carries many absurdities with it. For that particle "but if" [ἐὰν δὲ] in verse 15 would denote no connection. Second, "the Church" would denote some confused multitude. Third, what follows in verse 18 would have no connection with these words, contrary to the force of the words truly I say to you; see Matt. 5:26; 6:2; 8:10; 10:15; 11:11; 18:3; 19:23; Mark 10:15; 12:43; 13:30; Luke 12:37. (7.) To reprove would be to seek reconciliation. (8.) To sin against you would be the same as to suffer a personal injury.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Quòd autem dicit εἰπὲ τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ juvat scire quid nomine Ecclesiae intelligamus, nempe illos qui scilicet Ecclesiae gubernandae praesunt sed synecdochicè, ita hunc locum exponit Chrysostomus, homil. 16. in Matthaeum. Non ergo imus in castra Pontificiorum, qui censent hic per Ecclesiam significari Papam vel solum, vel cum concilio Episcoporum; qui dicunt, Papam propter obedientiae debitum, quod ipse dicit, pro judicio Ecclesiae totius habendum esse. Neque alia ratione aut interpretatione fieri potest, ut vox Ecclesiae videatur significare unum aut paucos homines: Sed, quum omnino non possit fieri, ut non tota fraternitas pro Ethnico aut Publicano habere teneatur eum, qui verae solidae redargutioni inobediens extiterit, manifestum est totius fraternitatis, qui praesunt scil. Ecclesiae gubernandae esse judicare de redargutione legitimâ & inobedientia ac contumacia ejus, qui à sermone aut facto malo aut scandaloso resipiscere non vult. Nec etiam militamus sub vexillo Erasti dicentis: Hoc, Dic Ecclesiae, non sumo, pro provocatione ad tribunal juridicum autoritatem in eos exercens, sed pro tertio ac ultimo charitatis gradu erga offendentem, quum scil. nec privata admonitio, nec coram testibus ad peccatorem emendandum satisfecerit, ut tunc vocetur selecta multitudo (quae est vis vocis ἐκκλησίας nativa) ut coram ea integra dissensionis causa exponatur, & ejus arbitrio referatur. ([1.) Q. Nunquam apud Matthaeum, imò nec in toto N.T. tale quid significat haec vox. (2.) Q. Pasor ex Suida duo concionum genera fuisse ostendit, alia νόμιμος ἐκκλησία dicta, concio legitima fixa & stata, quae ter singulis mensibus habebatur; alia convocata & indicta. (3.) Q. vox Hebraea קהל (quam saepissimè LXX. Interpretes vertunt
units.tr: As for the words εἰπὲ τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ [tell it to the Ecclesia], it helps to know what we understand by the name Ecclesia: namely, those who preside over the government of the Ecclesia, but used by synecdoche. So Chrysostom explains this passage in Homily 16 on Matthew. We therefore do not go over to the camp of the Papists, who hold that Ecclesia here means the Pope, either alone or with a council of bishops. They say that the Pope is to be taken as the judgment of the whole Church, because of the obedience owed to him. Nor can the word Ecclesia be made to mean one or a few men by any other reasoning or interpretation. Since it is quite impossible that the whole brotherhood should not be bound to regard as a heathen or tax collector the one who stubbornly refuses to heed a true and solid rebuke, it is plain that it belongs to the whole brotherhood, that is, to those who preside over the government of the Church, to judge of a lawful rebuke and of the disobedience and obstinacy of the man who will not repent of an evil or scandalous word or deed. Nor do we fight under the banner of Erastus, who says: "I do not take this 'tell the Church' as an appeal to a judicial tribunal, exercising authority over them, but as the third and last degree of love towards the offender, namely when neither private admonition nor admonition before witnesses has brought the sinner to amendment; then the chosen multitude (which is the natural force of the word ἐκκλησία) is to be called, so that the whole cause of the dispute may be set before it and be left to its judgment." (1) Objection: the word never has this meaning in Matthew, nor indeed anywhere in the New Testament. (2) Objection: Pasor, following Suidas, shows that there were two kinds of assemblies: one called νόμιμος ἐκκλησία [a lawful assembly], a fixed and appointed meeting held three times a month, and another that was called and announced. (3) Objection: the Hebrew word קהל [qahal], which the Seventy very often render by Ecclesia, and which occurs in this very passage of Matthew in the Hebrew edition, is used of elders and rulers: 1 Chronicles 13:2, 4; 29:1; 2 Chronicles 13; Deuteronomy 19:12, compared with Numbers 30:24; Joshua 20:4, 6; Exodus 12. So too the word עדה [edah] is used at Numbers 25:12 and Psalm 82:1. (4) Objection: Christ the Lord does not say "take the Ecclesia with you," as he had said before "take one or two with you," but "tell the Ecclesia," that is, a particular, settled and fixed Ecclesia, which can readily hear the case. (5) Objection: these three degrees are distinct. First there is private admonition, then public admonition before witnesses, and the third degree will be nothing unless it is the Ecclesia. (6) Objection: the word Ecclesia, as used by the seventy men, means the same as עדה and קהל. (7) Objection: Erastus himself, on page 225, confesses that the word Ecclesia is to be understood in the same sense as the Hebrew word קהל, or the Syriac word that answered to it in Christ's time. (8) Objection: the crowd frightens us away from the gloss of the great interpreters, Calvin, Pareus, Aretius, Beza and Diodati, especially since no argument can be drawn from the text itself that compels us to depart from the common meaning of the word. The word tradatur [be delivered] with τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ, in 1 Corinthians 5:5, means nothing other than exclusion from the Church. Since Christ reigns in the Church and the devil tyrannises outside it, it follows that those cast out by excommunication become the slaves of the devil. Because we are received into the communion of the Church on this condition, and remain in it, so that we are under the faith and protection of Christ, we say that the man cast out of the Church is in some sense delivered into the power of Satan. For he becomes a stranger and is alienated from the kingdom of Christ.

Collat. cum Num. 30. 24. Iof. 20. 4. 6. Exod. 12. Sic vox עדה Num. 25. 12. Pf. 82. 1. usurpatur.(4) Q. Christus Dominus non dicit assume tecum Ecclesiam, quemadmodum dixerat prius, assume tecum unum aut duos ; Sed dic Ecclesiæ, hoc est, certæ, statę ac fixę Ecclefię, quę causam audire in promptu est. (5.) Q. Hi tres gradus distinguuntur ; Etenim primò privata habetur admonitio, dein admonitio publica coram testibus : & tertius gradus nihil erit; nisi Ecclesia. (6.) Q. Vox Ecclesia à LXX. viris usurpata idem denotat, quod עדה & קהל (7.) Q. Ipsemet Erastus P. 225. eodem sensu vocem Ecclesiæ intelligendam esse fatetur, quo vox קהל aut Syriaca Christi tempore ei respondens.(8) Q. Ab hac Adversarii glossa interpretum clarissimorum Calvini, Parei, Aretii, Bezæ, Deodati nos terret multitudo, inprimis cùm ex ipso textu nullum argumentum adduci possit, quod nos à vocis communi acceptione cogat recedere, Et vox tradatur τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ, 1.Cor. 5. 5. nihil aliud innuit, quàm excludi ab Ecclesia, in qua cum Christus regnum obtineat, & extra eam Diabolus tyrannum agat, consequens est, ut qui inde eiiciuntur per excommunicationem, mancipia Diaboli efficiantur. Quia ergo hâc lege in communionem Ecclesiæ recipimur, & in ea manemus, ut sub fide, tutelaque Christi simus, dicimus eum qui extra Ecclesiam eiicitur, quodammodo Satanæ tradi in potestatem: extraneus enim fit, & alienatur à Christi regno.
units.tr: Others, however, understand "the Church" in this sense, as the word is used in the Hebrew text of this very passage of Matthew, and as it is applied to elders and rulers: 1 Chron. 13. 2, 4 and 29. 1; 2 Chron. 13; Deut. 19. 12, compared with Num. 30. 24; Josh. 20. 4, 6; Exod. 12. The word עדה [edah] is used in the same way at Num. 25. 12 and Ps. 82. 1. (4) Objection: Christ the Lord does not say "take the Church with you," as He had said before "take with you one or two," but "tell it to the Church," that is, to a definite, settled and fixed Church, to which the case can readily be reported. (5) Objection: these three degrees are distinct. First a private admonition is given, then a public admonition before witnesses, and the third degree would be nothing unless it were the Church. (6) Objection: the word Church, as used by the Seventy, denotes the same as עדה and קהל [qahal]. (7) Erastus himself confesses at p. 225 that the word Church must be understood in the same sense as the word קהל, or the Syriac word that corresponded to it at the time of Christ. (8) Objection: we are alarmed by the authority of this gloss of our adversary, given the multitude of most distinguished interpreters: Calvin, Pareus, Aretius, Beza and Diodati. This is especially so since no argument can be drawn from the text itself that compels us to depart from the common meaning of the word. The phrase "to deliver to Satan" (1 Cor. 5. 5) means nothing other than exclusion from the Church, in which Christ holds the kingdom and outside of which the Devil exercises his tyranny. It follows that those who are cast out of the Church by excommunication become the slaves of the Devil. Therefore, since by this law we are received into the fellowship of the Church and remain in it, so that we are under the faith and protection of Christ, we say that the man who is cast out of the Church is in some sense handed over to the power of Satan: for he becomes a stranger and is alienated from the kingdom of Christ.

units.la: Dicit quidem Erastus non audere se affirmare, Chorinthum illum fuisse Satanæ traditum, quoniam scribit in altera Epistola, ἐκαρὸν τῷ ζοιότῳ ἡ ἐπιτιμία αὕτη ἡ ὑπὸ τῶν πλειόνων sufficit illi homini increpatio à pluribus facta. Βι. At Sanctus Apostolus non scripsit ἐπιτίμησιν, sed ἐπιτιμίαν quam censuram interpretari optimè potes, & quia non jubet Apostolus increpari, sed Satanæ tradi. Corinthii magna tristitia affecti sunt ob hanc epistolam. Paulus quoque multis se excusat, quòd hunc Satanæ tradi statuisset, imò etiam se pœnituisse dicit. Certum est Corinthios doluisse de unius membri amputatione, erant etiam de salute ipsius soliciti, hoc enim charitas postulabat. Paulus se pœnituisse nusquam dicit, ut qui sibi sunt perperam factæ rei conscii: sed id egit quod veri Patres solent, si quando coacti sunt cum liberis dulcissimis severius agere: scientes quidem se
units.tr: Erastus indeed says that he does not dare to affirm that the Corinthian man was delivered to Satan, since in the second Epistle he writes: "ἱκανὸν τῷ τοιούτῳ ἡ ἐπιτιμία αὕτη ἡ ὑπὸ τῶν πλειόνων" [sufficient for such a man is this rebuke given by the many]. Reply: but the holy Apostle did not write ἐπιτίμησιν [a rebuke], but ἐπιτιμίαν [a censure], which you may rightly render as "censure," and he does not order the man to be rebuked but to be delivered to Satan. The Corinthians were greatly grieved by this letter. Paul also excuses himself at length for having decided that this man should be delivered to Satan, and even says that he regretted it. It is certain that the Corinthians grieved over the amputation of one member, and they were anxious for his salvation, for charity required this. Paul nowhere says that he repented, since he was conscious that he had acted wrongly; rather he did what true Fathers are wont to do when they have been compelled to deal more severely with their dearest children, knowing indeed

units.la: Nihil præter officium fecisse, sed nihilominus tamen apud se mœsti eventum rei expectantes, & quasi verentes ne quomodo modum excesserint. Affert Eras. Athanasii expositione etiam qui existimavit tradi Satanæ, hic, & aliis locis apud Apostolum, significare simile quidpiam quod Iobo factum est, quum Satanæ jus in illum aliquod, certis tamen finibus circumscriptum, tribueretur. Addit Augustinum & Chrysostomum non abhorruisse ab ea sententia. Si Athanasium acutiori mentis oculo perlustrabis, videbis expresse dicere exceptam fuisse animam, id est, vitam, sicut in Iobi tentatione factum est. Augustinus ita loquitur, ut nullus non videat in eorum ferri sententiam, qui ad carnis mortificationem referunt, quod de interitu carnis dicitur. Chrysostom. vero aperte ad cruciatum a Satana corpori inflictum refert, in Tim. 1. 20. & in Ioh. hom. 56. Eiiciebant, inquit, a communi fidelium cœtu, abscindebatur a grege, fiebat nudus, atque ita destitutus lupis patebat. Ergo nihil sequetur si dabimus, Satanæ traditos ab ipso fuisse obsessos, vel alio aliquo cruciatu, quasi vinculo a Satana constrictos fuisse, Luc. 13. 11. 16. id tamen fiebat, quòd extra territorium Ecclesiæ versarentur. Non multum laboramus etiam in significatione vocis ὀλεθρος, quâ perniciem, stragem, occisionem, mortem dicit significari. Q. Non simpliciter dicit Apostolus εἰς ὄλεθρον, sed addit τὴν σαρκὸς, ut nos doceat, quid deleri & perire velit, licet alibi non conjunxerit Apostolus ὄλεθρον cum τὴν σαρκὸς. obj. Si Satanæ tradere, est extra Ecclesiam eiicere, extra quam salus nulla est, non dixisset se hoc facere, ut salvus maneret in die judicii. Iam diximus quid nos, per tradi Satanæ intelligamus, nempe Satanæ tradi idem esse, atque ex Ecclesia, extra quam regnat Satan, ejectum declarari. Hinc comparantur excommunicati arescentibus palmitibus, & nisi caveant, tandem penitus amputandis, & in ignem coniiciendis: sed tamen ipsi viti adhuc adhærescentibus, & (sicut nos charitas bene sperare jubet) rursum aliquando succo vitis, suo tempore vivificandis. III. Ut Ira Dei tollatur ex Ecclesia. Nam supplicia illa quæ a Deo propter peccatum imminebant, sic evitantur & scandala tolluntur: Ecclesia quoque pura & immaculata conservabitur, præsertim non pollutis sacramentis. Sic enim cum maxima Dei contumelia & multorum offensione male audiret Ecclesia quasi esset quorumvis sceleratorum receptaculum, ut talia & similia vitemus stringamus gladium illum, qui nobis est traditus & Clavibus Regni Dei ita utamur, ut decet fidos clavigeros; ibi autem, ubi, vel Præsbyterium idoneum deest, vel non consentit in excommunicationem justam, solennis hic processus solet omitti: sed tamen bonus Pastor cum reliquis fidelibus Ecclesiæ membris, omni modo eò anniti debet, ut rei essentia conservetur, & scandala publicè arguantur ne iram provocent.
units.tr: that they have done nothing beyond their duty, and yet nonetheless anxious within themselves, awaiting the outcome of the matter, and as it were fearing lest they have somehow gone beyond the proper measure. Erastus cites the exposition of Athanasius, who thought that to be "delivered to Satan," here and in other places in the Apostle, signifies something like what happened to Job, when Satan was given some right over him, yet one circumscribed within certain limits. He adds that Augustine and Chrysostom did not shrink from that opinion. But if you examine Athanasius with a more penetrating mental eye, you will see that he expressly says that the soul, that is, the life, was excepted, as happened in the temptation of Job. Augustine speaks in such a way that everyone sees he is inclined to the opinion of those who refer what is said about the destruction of the flesh to the mortification of the flesh. Chrysostom clearly refers it to the torment inflicted on the body by Satan (on 1 Tim. 1. 20, and in homily 56 on John). "They cast him out," he says, "from the common assembly of the faithful; he was cut off from the flock, he was left naked, and so, abandoned, he lay open to the wolves." Therefore nothing follows if we grant that those delivered to Satan were in fact possessed by him, or afflicted with some other torment, as if bound by a chain by Satan (Luke 13. 11, 16). Yet this happened because they were living outside the territory of the Church. We do not labour much over the meaning of the word ὄλεθρος [olethros], which is said to signify ruin, destruction, slaughter or death. Objection: the Apostle does not simply say "for destruction," but adds "of the flesh," to teach us what he wishes to be destroyed and to perish, although elsewhere the Apostle did not join ὄλεθρος with "of the flesh." Objection: if to deliver to Satan is to cast out of the Church, outside of which there is no salvation, he would not have said that he did this so that the man might be saved on the day of judgement. We have already said what we understand by "delivered to Satan," namely that to be delivered to Satan is the same as being declared to have been cast out of the Church, outside of which Satan reigns. Hence excommunicated persons are compared to withering branches, which, unless they take care, will at last be wholly cut off and cast into the fire; yet they still cling to the vine, and (as charity bids us hope) will in due time be made alive again by the sap of the vine. III. That the wrath of God may be removed from the Church. For those punishments which God was threatening on account of sin are thus averted, and scandals are removed. The Church too will be preserved pure and unspotted, especially with its sacraments undefiled. For thus the Church would be evilly spoken of, with the greatest dishonour to God and offence to many, as if it were a receptacle of any wicked persons. So that we may avoid such things and similar ones, let us draw that sword which has been delivered to us, and use the Keys of the Kingdom of God as becomes faithful key-bearers. But where either a suitable Presbytery is lacking, or it does not agree to a just excommunication, this solemn process is commonly omitted. Nevertheless, the good Minister, together with the other faithful members of the Church, ought in every way to strive that the substance of the matter be preserved, and that scandals be publicly rebuked, lest they provoke wrath.
