units.la: Notandum etiam sensum horum verborum, ἐςω σοι ὥσπερ ὁ ἐθνι- κὸς καὶ ὁ τελώνης, non esse, nullum cum eo amplius habeto commercium. (1.) Q. Supponit haec interpretatio Iudæos cum Ethnicis nullam civilem communionem coluisse: At hoc falsum, Salomon enim coluit 1. Reg. 5. 18. 2. Paral. 1. 16. 17. & 11. 8. 17. & 9. 21. 28. Neh. 13. 16. 20. 21. (2.) Q. Viam sternit ad omnem evertendum ordinem, tam Ecclesiasticum, quàm politicum, necesse enim est ut ordo & pax corruat, ea sententia admissâ. Nec etiam est, judicio experitor coram Magistratu Ethnico, ut fingit Erastus, (1.) Q. Nullis Scripturæ testimoniis horum verborum significatio poterit probari. (2.) Q. Non lucrifaciendi fratrem offendentem docet modum; sed amissa recuperandi & injurias reparandi. Ergo dicimus habere pro Ethnico, esse eum pro tali habere, qui est extra Ecclesiam, seu non est Ecclesiæ membrum, utpote cui non licebat sanctuarium ingredi, quemadmodum Ethnicis præputiatis, Ezech. 44. 7. 9. Act. 21. 28. & 24. 6. qui sunt extra Ecclesiam, 1. Cor. 5. 1. Gal. 11. 15. Eph. 11. 11. 12. Col. 5. 12. 1. Thess. 4. 5. 1. Pet. 2. 11. & 4. 3. Hinc Dei populo opponuntur, Lev. 25. 42. 44. Matth. 4. 32. Actor. 4. 27. 1. Cor. 10. 32. Unde vox illa Ethnicus sumitur pro eo, qui est extra Ecclesiam, 2. Reg. 17. 8. & 21. 2. 2. Chron. 28. 3. & 33. 2. & 34. 14. Esd. 4. 21. Neh. 5. 8. Psal. 11. 1. & 79. 6. & 80. 8. & 135. 15. & 149. 7. Ier. 10. 2. Ezech. 11. 12. & 20. 9. 41. & 23. 30. Zach. 1. 15. Antequam determinemus quid sit aliquem habere pro Publicano, consultum duximus annotare, duo genera Publicanorum fuisse. Quidam enim erant justi & æqui, præter jus & æquum nihil prorsus exigentes: alii erant rapaces & iniqui, expilatores, quos hic nos intelligimus. Habere ergo pro Publicano aliquem est, 1. Ecclesiasticam cum eo communionem non colere. 2. Pro profano, flagitioso, ac ignominioso ducere. Hinc usurpatur hæc vox de pessimis peccatoribus, Matt. 5. 46. Luc. 18. 11. Publicani & Peccatores sæpius copulantur,
units.tr: It should also be noted that the sense of these words, "let him be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector" [ἔστω σοι ὥσπερ ὁ ἐθνικὸς καὶ ὁ τελώνης], is not "have no further dealings with him at all." (1.) This interpretation assumes that the Jews had no civil fellowship with the Gentiles. But this is false, for Solomon did maintain such fellowship: 1 Kings 5. 18; 2 Chron. 1. 16, 17; 8. 11, 17; 9. 21, 28; Neh. 13. 16, 20, 21. (2.) It clears the way for overturning every order, ecclesiastical as much as political, for if that opinion is admitted, order and peace must collapse. Nor does it mean, as Erastus imagines, that the matter is to be settled "by judgment before the heathen magistrate." (1.) No testimony of Scripture can prove this meaning of the words. (2.) The passage does not teach a way of winning over an offending brother, but of recovering what has been lost and repairing injuries. We therefore say that to hold someone as a Gentile is to regard as such one who is outside the Church, or is not a member of the Church, since he is not allowed to enter the sanctuary, just as the uncircumcised Gentiles were not (Ezek. 44. 7, 9; Acts 21. 28; 24. 6), and who are outside the Church (1 Cor. 5. 1; Gal. 11. 15; Eph. 11. 11, 12; Col. 5. 12; 1 Thess. 4. 5; 1 Pet. 2. 11; 4. 3). Hence they are set against the people of God (Lev. 25. 42, 44; Matth. 4. 32; Acts 4. 27; 1 Cor. 10. 32). From this the word "Gentile" is used of one who is outside the Church (2 Kings 17. 8; 21. 2; 2 Chron. 28. 3; 33. 2; 34. 14; Ezra 4. 21; Neh. 5. 8; Psal. 11. 1; 79. 6; 80. 8; 135. 15; 149. 7; Jer. 10. 2; Ezek. 11. 12; 20. 9, 41; 23. 30; Zech. 1. 15). Before we determine what it is to hold someone as a tax collector, we thought it useful to note that there were two kinds of tax collectors. Some were just and fair, demanding nothing beyond what was right and equitable; others were rapacious and unjust extortioners, and it is these we mean here. To hold someone as a tax collector is therefore (1.) not to keep ecclesiastical communion with him, and (2.) to regard him as profane, shameful and infamous. Hence the word is used of the worst sinners (Matth. 5. 46; Luke 18. 11). Tax collectors and sinners are often joined together,

units.la: Matth. 9. 10. & 11. 19. Marc. 11.15. Luc. 5. 30. & 16. 1. Sic copulantur Publicani & Meretrices, Matt. 21.31.
units.tr: Matth. 9. 10; 11. 19; Marc. 11. 15; Luke 5. 30; 16. 1. So tax collectors and harlots are joined together, Matth. 21. 31.

units.la: IX.
units.tr: IX.

units.la: ɣ A Causa formali, quæ est exclusio à communione Ecclesiæ, & participatione Sacrorum quæ in ea celebrantur. δ Ab adjuncta duratione, quoad resipuerit. Ergo ubi testimonium suæ pœnitentiæ dedit non est urgendus, si urgetur, rigor excedit modum, quâ in re nimia videtur fuisse Veterum austeritas, quæ mirum in modum erat periculosa. Pœnitentiam enim solemnem & privationem à sacra synaxi, nunc in tres annos, nunc in quatuor, nunc in septem, nunc in totam vitam indicabant. Quid hoc, quàm in magnum desperationis labyrinthum peccatorem detrudere? Cyprianus ad Cornelium Epist. 3. lib. 1. declarat se non fuisse tam rigidum. Patientia (inquit) & facilitas & humanitas nostra venientibus prasto est, opto omnes in Ecclesiam regredi: opto omnes commilitones nostros intra castra Christi, & Dei Patris domicilia concludi. Remitto omnia, multa dissimulo: studio & voto colligenda fraternitatis, etiam quæ in Deum commissa sunt non pleno judicio examino: ampleEtor prompta & plena dissimulatione cum pœnitentia revertentes, peccatum suum satisfactione humili & simplici confitentes. Sic Chrysostomus, Augustinus, proclives ad condonandum fuerunt. Hic enim schismaticum, post abjectum schisma & seriam pœnitentiam in Episcopatum recipere non dubitavit. Ex his videmus, quod debemus quidem esse rigidi Ecclesiasticæ disciplinæ observatores: sed ita ut multa dissimulemus, habentes in animo, quod Deus multa nobis condonat, unde Deus condonationum dicitur, Nch. 9. 17. Nec non illud quod ligationem excipit solutio.
units.tr: (1) From the formal cause, which is exclusion from the communion of the Church and from participation in the sacred rites celebrated in it. (2) From the adjunct of duration, namely, until he repents. Therefore, when he has given evidence of his repentance, he is not to be pressed further; if he is pressed, rigour exceeds due measure. In this matter the austerity of the ancients seems to have been excessive, and it was wonderfully dangerous. For they prescribed solemn repentance and deprivation of the holy assembly sometimes for three years, sometimes for four, sometimes for seven, sometimes for the whole of life. What is this but to thrust the sinner into a great labyrinth of despair? Cyprian, in his letter to Cornelius (Epist. 3, book 1), declares that he himself was not so harsh. "Patience," he says, "and gentleness and humanity are ready for those who come. I wish all to return to the Church; I wish all our fellow soldiers to be gathered within the camp of Christ and the dwelling of God the Father. I forgive everything, I overlook much; with zeal and desire to gather the brotherhood, I do not examine with full judgment even the offences committed against God. Let those who return with repentance be received with prompt and full forgiveness, confessing their sin by humble and simple satisfaction." So too Chrysostom and Augustine were inclined to pardon. For Augustine did not hesitate to receive a schismatic into the episcopate after he had cast off the schism and made serious repentance. From these examples we see that we ought indeed to be strict observers of ecclesiastical discipline, but in such a way that we overlook many things, bearing in mind that God forgives us many things; hence God is called the God of forgiveness (Neh. 9. 17). Likewise, loosing follows binding.

units.la: X.
units.tr: X.

units.la: iii. Ab oppositio, seu neglectu Censurarum Ecclesiasticarum. Quando primò censuræ non exercentur adversus magnos & notorios peccatores: sed perversi eorum mores tolerantur, quare damnatur Ecclesia Corinthiaca, propter ejus neglectum, 1. Cor. 5. 1.2. & acriter Pastor Tyatirensis reprehenditur, eò quòd sivit docere mulierem Iezabel, Apoc. 2. 20. Damnat & Origenes, hom. 7. Qui non succincti (inquit) Dei zelo, non imitantur Apostolum dicentem, tradidi hujusmodi hominem Satanæ: neque illud Evangelii implere studeut, ut peccatorem, qui non fuerit correptione Ecclesia emendatus, de de Ecclesia pulsum, velut gentilem habeant & publicanum, dum enim uni parcunt, universa Ecclesia moliuntur interitum, quibus statim addit: qua ista bonitas? qua ista misericordia? uni parcere & omnes indiscrimen adducere: polluitur enim ex uno peccatore populus, sicut ex ove morbida grex universus. Iuxta illud: Morbida sola pecus totum corrumpit ovile, Ne maculet alias est separanda grege.
units.tr: (iii.) From the opposite, or neglect, of ecclesiastical censures. The first case is when censures are not exercised against great and notorious sinners, but their wicked conduct is tolerated. For this reason the Church of Corinth was condemned for its neglect (1 Cor. 5. 1, 2), and the minister of Thyatira was sharply rebuked because he allowed the woman Jezebel to teach (Rev. 2. 20). Origen also condemns this in Homily 7: "Those who, not girded with zeal for God, do not imitate the Apostle saying, 'I have delivered such a man to Satan,' and do not strive to fulfil that saying of the Gospel, that a sinner who has not been amended by the correction of the Church should be cast out of the Church and be held as a Gentile and a tax collector. For while they spare one, they plot the destruction of the whole Church." And immediately he adds: "What kind of goodness is this? What kind of mercy is this? To spare one and bring everyone into danger! For the people is polluted by one sinner, as the whole flock is by one diseased sheep." Accordingly: "A single diseased sheep corrupts the whole fold, so it must be separated from the flock lest it infect the others."

units.la: Nec non illud Hieronymi, in illud Gal. 5. 9. Modicum fermenti totam massam corrumpit: Igitur, (inquit) scintilla statim, ut apparuit, extinguenda est, & fermentum a massa vicinia semovendum: secanda putrida carnes, & scabiosum animal a caulis ovium repellendum, ne tota domus, massa, corpus, & pecora, ardeat, corrumpatur, putrescat, intereat. Arius una scintilla fuit, sed quia non statim oppressa est, totum orbem ejus flamma populata est. Quando secundo, abutuntur πρὸς disciplina, qui abusus, tum in Diotrephe, 1. Ioh. 3. 10. tum in aliis, qui excommunicarunt Discipulos propter Christum, Luc. 6. 22. visus est.
units.tr: So too is that saying of Jerome on Gal. 5. 9, "A little leaven corrupts the whole lump." "Therefore," he says, "a spark must be extinguished as soon as it appears, and the leaven must be removed from the neighbouring mass; the rotten flesh must be cut away, and the scabby animal must be driven from the sheepfold, lest the whole house, mass, body and flock burn, be corrupted, rot and perish. Arius was one spark, but because it was not put out at once, his flame laid waste the whole world." The second case is when men abuse discipline; this abuse appeared both in Diotrephes (3 John 10) and in others who excommunicated the disciples for Christ's sake (Luke 6. 22).

units.la: XI.
units.tr: XI.

units.la: iv. A fine, eoque triplici, (1.) ut mala exempla tollantur ex Ecclesia. Videntes enim alii Ecclesiae cives timebunt, & in officio continebuntur, 1. Tim. 5. 20. Gal. 2. 14. (2.) Ut poenitentiam eamque seriam agant, quae judicio charitatis signa probabilia ostendat. Quod est ex conscientia peccati minus ante consideranti, mutata jam sententia, dolere. Quomodo μετάνοια frequentissime apud Graecos Autores pro poenitentia usurpatur; qua de re, eleganter Ausonius in Epigramate, de occasione & poenitentia dicit: Qua tibi juncta comes? Dicat tibi, dic rogo qua sis? Sum Dea, cui nomen nec Cicero ipse dedit. Sum Dea, qua facti non factique exigo poenas. Nempe ut poeniteat, sic Metanoea vocor.
units.tr: iv. The end, and this is threefold: (1) that bad examples may be removed from the Church. For the other citizens of the Church, seeing it, will fear and be kept in their duty, 1 Tim. 5:20; Gal. 2:14. (2) That they may undertake repentance, and a serious repentance, which shows probable signs of a judgment of charity. This is to grieve, having changed one's mind, over what one previously considered less serious, out of consciousness of sin. Thus metanoia is very often used in Greek authors for repentance. On this point Ausonius, in an epigram on Occasion and Repentance, speaks elegantly: "What companion is joined to you? Tell me, I beg, who are you? I am a goddess, to whom not even Cicero himself gave a name. I am a goddess who exacts penalties for what has been done and not done. Indeed, because I make a man repent, I am called Metanoea."

units.la: Certum quidem est apud Graecos μετανοεῖν, & μετάνοια generatim poenitere & poenitentiam notare; sive sit mali, sive boni, de secundo modo tamen certum est, frequentius intelligi, ut testatur Plutarchus, Περὶ ἠθυμίας: ὁ σύνεσις, ὅτι σύνοιδα δεινὰ ἐργασάμενος, οὗ ἔλεος ἐν σαρκὶ, τῇ ψυχῇ πῶς μετάμε λείαν αἱμασσέαν ἀεὶ, καὶ νύσσέαν, ἐπαπολείπει· τὰς μὲν γὰρ ἄλλας ἀναιρεῖ λύπας ὁ λόγος, πῶς δὲ μετάνοιαν αὐτὸς ἐργα-
units.tr: It is certain that among the Greeks metanoein and metanoia generally mean to repent and to signify repentance, whether of evil or of good. Yet it is certain that the second sense is the more frequent, as Plutarch testifies in his work On Peace of Mind: "Conscience, by which I am aware that I have done terrible things, leaves in the soul, as a sore in the flesh, a repentance that constantly stings and pricks. For reason removes other sorrows, but it is itself that produces repentance, by which the soul bites and punishes itself with shame" [ὁ σύνεσις, ὅτι σύνοιδα δεινὰ ἐργασάμενος, οὗ ἔλεος ἐν σαρκὶ, τῇ ψυχῇ πῶς μετάμε λείαν αἱμασσέαν ἀεὶ, καὶ νύσσέαν, ἐπαπολείπει· τὰς μὲν γὰρ ἄλλας ἀναιρεῖ λύπας ὁ λόγος, πῶς δὲ μετάνοιαν αὐτὸς ἐργα-].

units.la: { } Greek words set as printed; the final line is partly illegible. ζε) δαιμονιῶν σὺν αἰσχύνῃ τῆς ψυχῆς, καὶ κολαζομένῃ ὑπ᾽ αὐτῆς. Id est, Conscientia, qua conscius mihi sum perpetratorum scelerum, ut ulcus in carne, in anima poenitentiam cruentantem perpetuo ac vellicantem relinquit. Alias enim tristitias affert ratio: poenitentiam vero ipsa efficit, qua à seipsa cum pudore anima mordetur ac punitur. Verbalis enim poenitentiae professio non sufficit, quia sic sanctissima Dei instituta, ludibrio facile possent exponi, & actionis Ecclesiasticae virtus, in externa forma collocaretur.
units.tr: [ζε) δαιμονιῶν σὺν αἰσχύνῃ τῆς ψυχῆς, καὶ κολαζομένῃ ὑπ᾽ αὐτῆς.] That is: Conscience, by which I am aware of the wicked deeds I have committed, leaves in the soul, like an ulcer in the flesh, a repentance that wounds and gnaws continually. For reason brings other sorrows, but it is itself that produces repentance, by which the soul, with shame, is bitten and punished by itself. For a mere verbal profession of repentance is not enough, since in that case the most holy institutions of God could easily be exposed to mockery, and the force of ecclesiastical action would be placed in outward form.

units.la: XII.
units.tr: XII.

units.la: Duplex est Excommunicatio: Minor, vel Major, Levior, & Gravior. Minor, est abstentia sive suspensio ad tempus ab usu sacramentorum seu signorum gratiae Dei. De qua dicit Christus Dominus: Ne date quod sanctum est Canibus, Matth. 7. 6. Frustra hic Erastus nomine canum & porcorum nihil aliud vult significari, quàm sanae doctrinae ferociter resistentes. Nam hoc non obstat, quominus illi, qui vitae impuritate & nequitia se Canes & Porcos produnt & ostendunt, à Sacramentis, id est, sigillis rerum spiritualium arceri debeant. Fateor hoc discrime esse perdifficile cognitu, cùm & canes & porci aliquando mutentur in oves verbi praedicatione, & contra qui speciem ovis habebant, in canes & porcos degenerant. Ipsa igitur repudiatio doctrinae pertinax, satis superque detecta, porci & canis aliqua prodit indicia: Sic tamen incerta, ut non immerito Christus, regnum coelorum comparavit sagenae quidvis arripienti. Aliud autem de Sacramentis censendum est. Nam verbum Dei est veluti quoddam semen, quod satoribus in incertum eventum seritur. At Sacramenta, ut olim quidem sacrificia, nunc vero sancta Domini Coena, distinctam fidei professionem praesupponunt. Petrus Simonem ab impositione manuum prohibuit, cui tamen alterum, verbum scilicet resipiscentiae offert. Errat etiam in eo, quod dicat: canum & porcorum nomine intelligi posse & debere, hostes & persecutores Evangelii. (1.) Q. Porcos & canes dicimus illos, qui in sinu Ecclesiae versantur. (2.) Q. Hostes Ecclesiae, ut canes rabidos; & foedantes porcos vineam Domini, exterior professio non sublevat, imò nocentiores reddit, quòd Iesum profiteantur quidem ore, negent autem factis. Ismael enim & Esau circumcisi erant, & cum Abrahamo verum Deum extrinsecus agnoscebant: tamen exhaeredantur, ille quidem quòd cùm filius ancillae esset, benedictionis filium allatraret: iste vero quod profanus porcus esset, simplicem oviculam paratus dilaniare. Si Ecclesiæ domicilium, & fœderis tesseram terram Canaan, adeoque hæreditatis cœlestis typum, domum Abrahami & Isaaci fuisse non negaverimus: Hos duos Ismaelem & Esaum, Ecclesiæ excommunicationis vivum suis illis temporibus exemplum, & venturis seculis eosdem typos fuisse dabimus. Hæc excommunicatio viguit in veteri & meliori Ecclesia. Si quis enim aliquod perpetravit flagitium unde מבשור offendiculum exortum esset à sacræ cœnæ usu abstinebant: uti Theodosium Imperatorem Ambrosius ob eadem Thessalonicæ patratam. Qui dum videret se jure communione esse privatum, stravit omne quo circundatus erat insigne regium: & deflevit publice peccatum suum, quod fraude aliorum irrepserat, & sic gemitu & lacrymis oravit veniam, de quo Poeta:
units.tr: Excommunication is twofold: minor or major, lighter and heavier. The minor is the abstention, or suspension for a time, from the use of the sacraments, that is, the signs of God's grace. Of this the Lord Christ says: Do not give what is holy to dogs, Matt. 7:6. Erastus here vainly maintains that by the names of dogs and swine nothing else is meant than those who fiercely resist sound doctrine. For this does not prevent those who reveal and show themselves to be dogs and swine by the impurity and wickedness of their lives from being kept away from the sacraments, that is, the seals of spiritual things. I admit that this distinction is very difficult to recognise, since dogs and swine are sometimes changed into sheep by the preaching of the word, and on the contrary those who had the appearance of sheep degenerate into dogs and swine. Obstinate rejection of doctrine, therefore, when it has been sufficiently and more than sufficiently exposed, does reveal some signs of the swine and the dog. Yet these signs are so uncertain that Christ not unreasonably compared the kingdom of heaven to a net that gathers up all kinds of things. But something else must be judged concerning the sacraments. For the word of God is like a seed, which is sown by the sowers with an uncertain outcome. But the sacraments, as formerly the sacrifices and now the holy Supper of the Lord, presuppose a distinct profession of faith. Peter forbade Simon from the laying on of hands, yet offered him something else, namely the word of repentance. Erastus is also wrong in saying that by the name of dogs and swine enemies and persecutors of the Gospel can and must be understood. (1) We call dogs and swine those who live within the bosom of the Church. (2) As for the enemies of the Church, like rabid dogs, and swine that defile the vineyard of the Lord, an outward profession does not help them; rather it makes them more guilty, because they profess Jesus with their mouth but deny him by their deeds. For Ishmael and Esau were circumcised, and with Abraham they acknowledged the true God outwardly; yet they were disinherited, the one because, being the son of a servant, he mocked the son of the blessing, and the other because, being a profane swine, he was ready to tear apart a simple little sheep. If we do not deny that the dwelling place of the Church and the token of the covenant, the land of Canaan, and so the type of the heavenly inheritance, was the house of Abraham and Isaac, we shall grant that these two, Ishmael and Esau, were a living example of excommunication in their own times and types of the same in the ages to come. This excommunication flourished in the old and better Church. For if anyone had committed some scandal from which a stumbling-block [מכשול] arose, they abstained from the use of the sacred Supper, as Ambrose did with the Emperor Theodosius for the same deed done at Thessalonica. When he saw that he had been deprived of communion by right, he laid aside all the royal insignia with which he was surrounded, and publicly lamented his sin, which had crept in through the deceit of others, and so with groans and tears he begged pardon, of which the poet says:

units.la: O nimium dilecte Deo, cui militat æther,
units.tr: O you, too dear to God, for whom the heavens fight,

units.la: Et conjurati veniunt ad Classica venti.
units.tr: And the winds come, sworn, at the summons of the trumpets.

units.la: Non enim debent dedecori putare Reges magni & Principes potentes, si coram Christo Rege Regum, 1. Tim. 6. 15. Apoc. 14. 14. se se prosternant & delicti veniam petant. Erastus tamen obj. Patres omnes de eadem spirituali esca ederunt, & ex eodem spiritupotu biberunt, inter quos idololatræ, scortatores, tentatores, murmuratores fuerunt. At illa Apostolica verba applicari possunt nobis, qui omnes de uno pane edimus, & de eodem poculo bibimus. Peculiari ratione hoc factum est, quod omnes etiam indignissimi Manna ederint, & ex rupis aqua biberint, quæ nec in sacrificiis veterum nec in nostris habet locum. Licet enim fuerunt Spiritualium rerum typi, atque adeo ipsius Christi; sic tamen illæ res spirituales fuerunt typi rerum spiritualium, & ipsius Christi, ut essent interea beneficia corporalia, universo populo ad pascendum destinata, minimè ergo convenit recensere inter illa, quæ solum fuerunt sacramenta.(2.)Deus illos punivit perdendo eos in deserto, paucis relictis, quod autem fuerint negligentes, ideo factum est, quia errantium multitudo hoc postulabat, ne rigidi essent, sed remissiores aliquantulum.
units.tr: For great kings and powerful princes ought not to think it a disgrace, if before Christ, the King of kings, 1 Tim. 6:15; Rev. 14:14, they prostrate themselves and ask pardon for their offence. Erastus objects, however, that all the Fathers ate of the same spiritual food and drank of the same spiritual drink, among whom were idolaters, fornicators, tempters and murmurers. But those apostolic words can be applied to us, who all eat of one bread and drink from the same cup. This happened for a special reason: that all, even the most unworthy, ate manna and drank from the water of the rock, which has no place either in the sacrifices of the ancients or in ours. For although these were types of spiritual things, and indeed of Christ himself, yet those spiritual things were types of spiritual things, and of Christ himself, in such a way that meanwhile they were corporal benefits destined for the whole people for their nourishment. It is by no means fitting, therefore, to count these among those things which were only sacraments. (2) God punished them by destroying them in the wilderness, with only a few left; and that they were negligent was indeed because the multitude of wanderers demanded this, so that the leaders would not be harsh but somewhat more lenient.

units.la: XIII.
units.tr: XIII.

units.la: Hactenus de Excommunicatione Minore, sequitur, ut agamus, de Majore, cujus tres sunt gradus. [1.] Est Excommunicatio simplex. Qua homo impius à communi coetu seu consortio fidelium amovetur, unde ab Hebraeis נדה dicitur Zach. 14. 11. Esa. 66. 5. Neh. 13. 13. id est, remotio, separatio, à Graecis ἀφορισμὸς, Luc. 6. 22. Cui respondet Phrasis illa Graeca ἀποσυνάγωγος γίνεσθαι, synagogâ moveri, Ioh. 9. 22. & 12. 42. & 16. 2. [2.] Anathema quod Graeci vocant donarium, sive dicatum, quod templorum aerariis consecratur, ὥσπερ τὸ ἀνατιθέναι, quod solebat dedicari, aut de columnis aut parietibus suspendi, unde Templum Hyerosolimitanum dicitur ἀνα-θήματα ornatum, Luc. 21. 5. Nempe phialis, aureis, argenteis, tripodibus, corollariis, quod nos hic non intelligimus. Sed ἀνάθεμα ab eodem verbo derivatum, diversae tamen significationis, quod Hebraei חרם appellant, à quibus ad Ecclesias Christianas translata est, & facta est iis tam nota & familiaris, ut Amen, Alleluia, Hosanna. Origenes facit mentionem istius anathematis, ad quaest. 121. de differentia ἀναθεματισμὸς & καταθεματισμὸς, cum inquit. Ἀνάθεμα λέγεται τὸ ἀνακείμενον ἢ ἀφορισμένον Θεῷ εἰς κοινὴν χρῆσιν μηκέτι λαμβανόμενον ἢ τὸ ἀπηλλοτριωμένον Θεῷ διὰ κακίαν. Anathema dicitur, quod repositum & separatum Deo, & in communem usum, non amplius accipitur: aut id, quod à Deo per malitiam est abalienatum. Hic gradus ita definitur. Quo peccator à consortio fidelium non solùm summovetur: sed etiam pronunciatur alienus ab Ecclesia, Matt. 18. 17. Gal. 1. 8. [3.] Anathema Maranatha, 1. Cor. 16. 21. Quo is, qui est inemendabilis & desperatus, aeterno exitio devovetur, sive haereticus, sive facinorosus, quae est, ultima execratio, cujus ut non ita nobis est nota ratio: ita etiam usus rarissimus esse debet. Hujus facit mentionem Chrysostomus, exponens ad Rom. cap. 9. v. 1. Cum dicit τὶ ἐν ἔχῃ ἀνάθεμα, ἀυτὸς ἀνὴρ λέγοντος, εἴτις ἐ φιλεῖ τὸν κύριον Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν, ἔσω ἀνάθεμα, τελέσει κεχωρισμένος πάντων, ἀλλὰ ὡς ἔσω πάντων, καθάπερ γὰρ τὸ ἀναθήματος τὸ ἀνατιθέμενον Θεῷ εἰδεὶς ἂν τολμήσειν ἀπλῶς τὴν χεῖρα ἁψασθαι, ὥστε... ANATHEMATI, τιμῆς ἕνεκα ὑδεὶς ἐτόλμα ἐκχωρεῖν... ὁ τρόπος τῆς χωρισμοῦ ἐχ εἰς ἀλλὰ ἢ ἐναντίος ἐκείνῃ, τῆς μὲν γὰρ ἀπεικοντὶ ὡς ἀνακει-μένῳ. μὲνῦ θεῷ τῇ ῇ, ὡς ἀλλοτριωμένῃ θεῷ κηΐ δὲ ῥραγμάτος ἐξ ἐλπίας. In V. T. habemus hujus anathematizationis exem-pla in Core, Datan & Abiram, Num. 16. 32. Ios. 7. 7. & in N. T. 2. Tim. 4. 14. Gal. 5. 12. Hanc vocem Maranatha Tertullianus legit Chaldaicè מרנא אתא cap. 14. de Pudicit. ubi ʜ post vocem Marana absorberi docet speciem extremi anathematis designans, Sed vox ista nobis videtur magis esse Syriaca quâ lingua Apostoli loquebantur, ut sit idem quod Dominus venit Syris enim Maran est Dominus.
units.tr: So far concerning the Lesser Excommunication. It follows that we treat of the Greater, which has three degrees. [1.] The first is simple excommunication, by which a wicked man is removed from the common assembly or fellowship of the faithful. The Hebrews call it נדה (Zech. 14. 11; Isa. 66. 5; Neh. 13. 13), that is, removal or separation, and the Greeks call it ἀφορισμός (Luke 6. 22). To this corresponds the Greek phrase ἀποσυνάγωγος γίνεσθαι, to be put out of the synagogue (John 9. 22; 12. 42; 16. 2). [2.] Anathema: the Greeks call a votive offering or dedicated object, which is consecrated to the treasuries of temples, a donarium, as ἀνατιθέναι was the custom, namely to hang things up on columns or walls. Whence the Jerusalem Temple is said to be adorned with ἀναθήματα (Luke 21. 5), that is, with bowls, golden and silver vessels, tripods and garlands, which we do not need to understand here. But ἀνάθεμα, derived from the same verb though with a different meaning, which the Hebrews call חרם, was carried over from them into the Christian churches and became as familiar to them as Amen, Alleluia and Hosanna. Origen mentions this anathema in question 121, on the difference between ἀναθεματισμός and καταθεματισμός, when he says: "Ἀνάθεμα is said of what is dedicated and set apart to God for common use and no longer taken back, or of what has been alienated from God through wickedness." This degree is defined thus: by it a sinner is not only removed from the fellowship of the faithful but is also declared a stranger to the Church (Matt. 18. 17; Gal. 1. 8). [3.] Anathema Maranatha (1 Cor. 16. 21): by it the one who is incorrigible and beyond hope is consigned to eternal destruction, whether he be a heretic or a criminal. This is the last curse, and although its nature is not so well known to us, its use ought to be very rare. Chrysostom makes mention of it in his exposition of Rom. 9. 1, where he says that to have an anathema is to say, "If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be anathema," and that he is then separated from all, not as one above all but as one among all. For just as no one would dare simply to touch a thing dedicated to God, out of reverence no one would venture to approach it... the manner of separation is not toward one thing but the opposite of that: the one is set apart as dedicated to God, the other as alienated from God [ἀνάθεμα, ἀνακείμενον]. In the Old Testament we have examples of this anathematizing in Korah, Dathan and Abiram (Num. 16. 32) and in Joshua 7. 7; in the New Testament, in 2 Tim. 4. 14 and Gal. 5. 12. Tertullian reads this word Maranatha in Chaldee as מרנא אתא in chapter 14 of On Modesty, where he teaches that the ח is swallowed after the word Marana, designating a kind of extreme anathema. But this word seems to us rather Syriac, the language the Apostles spoke, so that it means the same as "the Lord has come", for Maran in Syriac means Lord.

units.la: XIV.
units.tr: XIV.

units.la: Primo gradu excommunicationis utitur Ecclesia adversus pravam vitam. Secundo adversus falsa dogmata. Huc pertinet illud: quod olim in pravorum dogmatum Autores & Doctores mos erat pronunciare in synodis, ubi qnum pravum aliquod dogma damnabatur. Solebat unus ex Episcopis altâ voce pronunciare. Si quis ita sentiat & doceat anathema sit, cæteri autem Episcopi clamarunt. Anathema sit, ut Hieronymus Dialog. adversus Lucifer. refert ex actis Synodi Ariminensis, Socrates Histor. Ecclesiast. lib. 7. cap. 33. de anathemate, ὅτω γὰρ καλεῖν εὐθαμὲν τὸν κατὰ τῆς βλασφημίας ῥῆφον ὅζων αὐτῷ ὡσπερ ἐν ςήλῃ ἀνασηλῶντες φανερὰν ταῖς ἁπασι κηρύσσομεν. Sic sententiam contra alicujus blasphemiæ autorem solemus appellare pronunciatam, quando eam proinde notam facimus omnibus, ac si in columella incisa, in loco publice collocaretur. Tertio gradu utimur adversus eos, qui in Spiritum Sanctum peccant.
units.tr: First, the Church uses the first degree of excommunication against a wicked life. Second, it uses it against false doctrines. To this belongs the custom that once existed among the authors and teachers of wicked doctrines, of making a proclamation in synods when some wicked doctrine was condemned. One of the bishops would pronounce in a loud voice, "If anyone thinks and teaches this way, let him be anathema," and the other bishops would shout, "Let him be anathema." Jerome reports this in his Dialogue against the Luciferians from the acts of the Synod of Ariminum, and Socrates, Ecclesiastical History book 7 chapter 33, speaks of the anathema: "For thus we are accustomed to call the sentence pronounced against the author of some blasphemy, when we make it known to all, as if it were carved on a pillar and set up publicly in a place" [ὅτω γὰρ καλεῖν εὐθαμὲν τὸν κατὰ τῆς βλασφημίας ῥῆφον ὅζων αὐτῷ ὡσπερ ἐν ςήλῃ ἀνασηλῶντες φανερὰν ταῖς ἁπασι κηρύσσομεν]. Third, we use it against those who sin against the Holy Spirit.

units.la: XV.
units.tr: XV.

units.la: Ex his Excómunicatio Major est, quâ is qui frater nominatur propter doctrinæ ac vitæ gravem impuritatem, post monitiones Ecclesiæ privatas & publicas contemptas, & in peccato suo contumax non tantùm à privilegiis Ecclesiæ, sed etiam ab Ecclesiæ communione ut tabidum membrum, quod pestem suam partibus etiam synceris afferre posset eiicitur. Nam hæc est ad deviandum nostra protervitas, ut nihil familiarius sit, quàm malis exemplis, homines à recto vitæ cursu abduci. Hunc usum Apostolus notavit, cùm incestuosum jubet amandari à Corinthiis, 1.Cor. 5. 6. & quasi ense spirituali resecari. Claves enim Ministrorum spirituales non carnales sunt, 2. Cor. 12. 4. Nos dum in corpore nostro, aliquid quod reliquo corpori nocea̅t sentimus ; uri & secari patimur membrū aliquod, potiùs quàm totum corpus intereat. Nec hæc excommunicatio omne postliminii jus intercludit, ut ad pœnitentiam & peccatorum ἐξομολόγησιν redeat, per quam semper ad cœlestem Ierusalem reditus datur, supremam ergo inerrantem fratrem sententiam ingeminare, & Pontificiis devotionibus uti, qua peccatori omnis spes abscinditur, penes homines, vel aliquem hominum (ut supra dictum) non est.
units.tr: Of these, there is major excommunication, by which a man who is called a brother, on account of grave impurity of doctrine or life, after private and public admonitions of the Church have been despised, and who is stubborn in his sin, is cast out not only from the privileges of the Church but from the communion of the Church itself, like a rotting member that could spread its plague even to the sound parts. For our perversity is such that nothing is more familiar to us than being led from the right course of life by bad examples. The Apostle noted this use when he orders the incestuous man to be put away by the Corinthians, 1 Cor. 5:5, 6, and to be cut off as with a spiritual sword. For the keys of the ministers are spiritual, not carnal, 2 Cor. 10:4. When we feel in our body something that would harm the rest of the body, we allow a member to be burned and cut, rather than the whole body to perish. Nor does this excommunication cut off every right of return, so that he may come back to repentance and the confession of sins [ἐξομολόγησιν], through which a way back to the heavenly Jerusalem is always open. Therefore to repeat the supreme sentence against the brother as if it were infallible, and to use the devotions of the Papists, by which all hope is cut off from the sinner, is not within the power of men or of any man (as said above).

units.la: XVI.
units.tr: XVI.

units.la: Vsus excommunicationis, non versatur circa infirmitates illas, quæ sunt omnium Christianorum communes. Secus enim omnes deberent excommunicari. Sunt enim omnes infirmitatibus circumsepti, non solùm impii, sed etiam renati, Iob. 4. 18. 19. Iac. 3. 2. In multis impingimus omnes. Non etiam [2] versatur circa atrocia illa crimina, quæ legibus humanis solent coerceri: quia disciplina Ecclesiastica, pars est regni Christi, & proinde spiritualem habet naturam: sed fit propter illa peccata ad quæ expianda extraordinaria pœnitentia est opus, seu propter scandalum datum fratri, Matth. 18. 15. ut alii in cursu pietatis inoffenso pede pergant. Sufficit enim privatim & publicè monuisse, contra veteres Novitianos & recentes Memnonitas, seu Anabaptistas, qui primò hominem excommunicant & demum admonent. Volunt enim ut extra Ecclesiam pœnitentiam agat, non intra & quidem. Ex Lev. 10. 1. 2. Nadah & Abihu sine prævia admonitione flammâ Dei exanimati, & mortui sunt coram Iehova. Et ex 2. Sam. 6. 7. Huzam Deus percussit, ut moreretur propter extensionem manuum suarum ad arcam Dei. Sed errant. Quia hæc fuerunt extraordinaria Dei judicia, adeoque vindictæ & justitiæ Dei exempla, quæ ab Ecclesia ad ordinarium suum processum cum transgressoribus trahenda non sunt, quia secus posset Ecclesia supplicio capitis afficere sontes, quod Anabaptista ne Magistratui quidem largiuntur: Nos ergo qui in Iesu Christi schola didicimus, excommunicationi admonitiones tum privatas, tum publicas præmittamus, & quidem cum mansuetudine & longanimitate. Medicina enim proportionem debet habere ad morbum cui tollendo inservit.
units.tr: The use of excommunication does not concern those weaknesses which are common to all Christians. Otherwise all would have to be excommunicated. For all are beset by infirmities, not only the ungodly but also the regenerate, Job 4:18, 19; James 3:2: In many things we all stumble. Nor does it concern those atrocious crimes which are usually punished by human laws, because ecclesiastical discipline is a part of the kingdom of Christ and therefore has a spiritual nature. It is applied rather on account of those sins for which extraordinary repentance is needed to make atonement, or on account of scandal given to a brother (Matt. 18:15), so that others may continue in the course of piety without stumbling. For it is enough to admonish privately and publicly, against the ancient Novatians and the recent Memnonites, or Anabaptists, who first excommunicate a man and only afterwards admonish him. For they want him to do penance outside the Church, not within it. From Lev. 10:1, 2, Nadab and Abihu were struck dead by the fire of God without any prior admonition, and died before Jehovah. And from 2 Sam. 6:7, God struck Uzzah so that he died because of stretching out his hands to the ark of God. But they are wrong. For these were extraordinary judgments of God, and thus examples of the vengeance and justice of God, which the Church is not to draw into its ordinary process against offenders, since otherwise the Church could inflict capital punishment on the guilty, which the Anabaptists do not even grant to the magistrate. We, therefore, who have learned in the school of Jesus Christ, should send admonitions, both private and public, before excommunication, and indeed with gentleness and patience. For a remedy ought to be proportioned to the disease it is meant to cure.

units.la: XVII.
units.tr: XVII.

units.la: Excommunicatio separat excommunicatum à communione Sanctorum, quam duplicem statuit Scriptura. Ecclesiasticam & Politicam. Illa est, quæ in Ecclesiæ externa communione, sacramentis, & omnibus aliis pietatis exercitiis, consistit, ab his, quatenus divinæ gratiæ sunt signa peculiaria seu Tesseræ militares, quibus Ecclesiæ militaris membra distinguuntur à Iudæis & Gentilibus, Christi signa non sequentibus. Separamus excommunicatum, utpote qui enormiter peccavit, ad eosdem enim singulares homines, qui constituunt Ecclesiam in proprietate sua spectant, Ioh. 17. 9. 10. 11. Ergo, ex natura rei, patet separari ab hac communione, quia propria est fidelium & sanctorum. Declarat enim homo peccato deditus, se haberi pro Ethnico & Publicano, Matth. 18. 17. Hæc quæ in omni voluntaria & libera conversatione, quâ singularis animi propensio, in personam alterius, & status ejus approbatio declarari solet, consistit, quæ vitari debet, 1. Cor. 5. 11. 2. Thess. 3. 14. Officium enim fidelium est, cum consortio eorum sit rejectus, ut sese separent, ut salutaris ipsi incutiatur pudor. Ita enim conducit illi suam nequitiam castigare, quâ expergefiat, id indigitat Apostolus, cum in hunc modum loquitur, Si quis non obedit doctrinæ nostræ, hunc notate, & ne commisceamini cum illo, Rom. 16. 17. 1. Cor. 5. 11. & vetus Regula Canonistarum prohibet: Os, orare, vale, communio, mensa negatur.
units.tr: Excommunication separates the excommunicated person from the communion of the saints, a communion which Scripture sets out in two kinds: ecclesiastical and political. The first consists in the external communion of the Church, in the sacraments and all the other exercises of piety. It is withheld from such a person insofar as these are the particular signs of divine grace, or the military tokens by which the members of the militant Church are distinguished from Jews and Gentiles, who do not follow the signs of Christ. We separate the excommunicated person because he has sinned outrageously. These individuals, who make up the Church, are the ones considered in their own proper character (John 17:9, 10, 11). Hence, by the nature of the thing, it is plain that he must be cut off from this communion, since it belongs properly to the faithful and the saints. A man given over to sin declares that he is to be regarded as a Gentile and a tax collector (Matt. 18:17). This is to be avoided, namely in every voluntary and free association by which a particular inclination of the mind, or approval of another person and his condition, is usually shown (1 Cor. 5:11; 2 Thess. 3:14). For it is the duty of the faithful, once he has been rejected by their fellowship, to hold themselves apart, so that a wholesome shame may be struck into him. For it helps him to rebuke his own wickedness, so that he may be roused from it. The Apostle points to this when he speaks in this manner: If anyone does not obey our teaching, mark him, and do not associate with him (Rom. 16:17; 1 Cor. 5:11). And the old rule of the canonists forbids it: Let him be denied speech, prayer, greeting, fellowship, and table.

units.la: Non autem vel Politica, vel Oeconomica illa communio, quæ pa vinculum obligationis habet, à lege Naturæ, qualis est Mariti & Vxoris, Parentum & Liberorum, Dominorum & Servorum, Principum & Subditorum, quam tum Scriptura S. tum Natura, tum publica Iura flagitant, est separanda. 1. Cor. 7. 4. 5. 2. Cor. 2. 8. Non igitur cessandum est à monendo, docendo, corripiendo, neque à cibando, potando, si necessitas urserit; sed tentanda omnia quibus si fieri possit in viam redeat. Vltra enim excommunicatio non se extendit, quàm præcepta Dei & charitas patiuntur, & sic fit זהב gladius medicinalis, non רע hostis. Et Christus Dominus quosdam vult haberi, ut Publicanos, quosdam ut Ethnicos, inter quos sunt, quorum spectari potest resipiscentia, & reditus in Ecclesiam: Christus Dominus etiam cum Publicanis & Peccatoribus accubuisse legitur, Matth. 9. 10. 11. & 11. 19. Marc. 2. 15. 16. Luc. 5. 30.
units.tr: However, that political or domestic fellowship which has the bond of obligation from the law of nature, such as that of husband and wife, parents and children, masters and servants, rulers and subjects, is not to be separated. Holy Scripture, nature, and public law all demand this (1 Cor. 7:4, 5; 2 Cor. 2:8). Therefore we must not cease from admonishing, teaching, and correcting him, nor from feeding and giving him drink if necessity presses. Rather, every means must be tried by which, if possible, he may return to the right way. For excommunication does not extend further than the precepts of God and charity allow. Thus it becomes a medicinal sword [חרב], not an enemy [רע]. Christ the Lord also wishes some to be regarded as tax collectors, and others as Gentiles; among these are those whose repentance and return to the Church may be looked for. It is read that Christ the Lord also reclined at table with tax collectors and sinners (Matt. 9:10, 11; 11:19; Mark 2:15, 16; Luke 5:30).

units.la: & & 7. 34. 35. 36. & 18. 13. & 19. 2. quem actum Scribæ & Pharisæi admirabantur & dixerunt, quid est quod cum Publicanis & Peccatoribus edit, bibit, Marc. 2. 16. Respondit ℣. 17. & dicit. Qui valent non opus est medico: sed iis qui male se habent: Non veni ut vocarem justos; sed peccatores ad resipiscentiam. Incumbit ergo unicuique Christiano, ut talem admoneat, cibet, & alia necessaria suppeditet.
units.tr: And at 7:34, 35, 36; 18:13; and 19:2, which act the scribes and Pharisees marvelled at, saying, Why does he eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners? (Mark 2:16). He answered (v. 17) and said: Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are ill do. I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance. Therefore it falls to every Christian to admonish such a person, to feed him, and to supply his other necessities.

units.la: XVIII.
units.tr: XVIII.

units.la: Hinc errant Anabaptistæ, omne commercium cum ipsis negantes. Imò conjugibus conjugalia, parentibus debita à filiis negantes, qui legem Dei perversa superstitione evacuant. 1. Quia Moralia & Naturalia per excommunicationem non corrumpuntur, Matth. 7. 11. & 15. 4. 5. 1. Cor. 7. 12. 13. 16. Si quis uxorem habet infidelem quæ consentiat, ad habitandum cum eo, ne eam dimittito, de viro similiter loquitur ℣. 13. Quibus verbis docet nullam esse causam dubitandi, de matrimonii indissolubilitate. Nam inter Iudæos & eos qui ad Christianam fidem se applicuerant matrimonia esse rata, quemadmodum Apostolus docet ex Sermone Christi indissolubilia, seu tam firma & constitutione Dei inter conjuges munita: ut non sine scelere magno, conjugium dirimi possit.
units.tr: The Anabaptists err here, denying all fellowship with such people. Indeed, they deny to spouses their conjugal rights, and to parents the duties owed by their children, and by a perverse superstition they nullify the law of God. First, because moral and natural duties are not corrupted by excommunication (Matt. 7:11; 15:4, 5; 1 Cor. 7:12, 13, 16). If anyone has an unbelieving wife who consents to live with him, let him not put her away; he speaks similarly of the husband in v. 13. By these words he teaches that there is no reason to doubt the indissolubility of marriage. For among the Jews, and among those who had come to the Christian faith, marriages were held valid, just as the Apostle teaches, from the words of Christ, that they are indissoluble, that is, so firm and so fortified by the ordinance of God between the spouses that a marriage cannot be dissolved without great wickedness.

units.la: 2. Quia ceremonialia & ritualia debent cedere moralibus, seu legem charitatis præcedere debere, legem cæremonialem, quod probat Christus Dominus in refutatione Pharisæorum, Matth. 12. 3. 4. Nonne legistis (inquit) quid fecerit David 1. Sam. 21. 4. 5. 6. cum esuriret ipse, & qui erant cum eo? Quomodo intravit in domum Dei & panes propositionis ederit, quibus vesci non erat ipsi licitum, neque iis qui cum eo erant, sed Sacerdotibus solis? Lev. 24. 9.
units.tr: Second, because ceremonial and ritual matters ought to yield to moral ones, or the law of charity ought to take precedence over the ceremonial law. Christ the Lord proves this in his refutation of the Pharisees (Matt. 12:3, 4). Have you not read, he says, what David did (1 Sam. 21:4, 5, 6) when he was hungry, he and those who were with him? How did he enter the house of God and eat the bread of the presentation, which it was not lawful for him to eat, nor for those who were with him, but for the priests alone? (Lev. 24:9).

units.la: XIX.
units.tr: XIX.

units.la: Detestamur etiam impium fulmen & Anathema magnæ illius meretricis Apoc. 17. 15. & 19. 2. & asseclarum ejus, quo Reges Evangelicos Regno exuere, populos seu Ecclesias reformatas sacramento solvere & omnem societatem turbare contendunt, contra doctrinam Apostoli, Rom. 13. 1. 1. Tim. 2. 1. 2. Nec non, quo integra Regna & Provincias à sacris arcere solent. Q. est illegitima & ipso jure nulla, sive [1] Excommunicantis personam, sive [2] Ipsam per se excommunicationem, sive excommunicatos ab ipso, spectes,
units.tr: We also detest the impious thunderbolt and anathema of that great harlot (Apoc. 17. 15. & 19. 2.) and of her adherents, by which they strive to strip Evangelical kings of their kingdoms, to dissolve the sacrament for the reformed peoples or Churches, and to disturb all society, contrary to the doctrine of the Apostle (Rom. 13. 1. 1. Tim. 2. 1. 2.). Nor do we accept the practice by which they are wont to bar whole kingdoms and provinces from sacred things. It is illegitimate and void in law, whether you look at (1) the person of the excommunicator, or (2) excommunication itself, or the excommunicated persons themselves.

units.la: Quia si consideres excommunicantis personam, jure ipsos Evangelicos Papa excommunicare non potest: In causa enim Reformatorum est judex incompetens & suspectus; Primo quia est hostis Capitalis. Testatur hoc abunde ipsa Hispanica inquisitio jussu Papæ introducta. Pleno gutture clamant tot lanienæ in Francia. Evincunt bella in multis Regnis & Provinciis accensa, (loquere pro me hodie, dulcissima Patria Hungaria, quæ ab ipso reformationis exordio, ad hæc usque tempora, hunc ignem à Papa accensum ferre coacta es, & modò portare cogeris.) Planum faciunt ab ipso publicatæ condemnationes adversus Reformatos. Confirmant acta hostilia Regibus, Principibus, data contra Evangelicos. Demonstrant consultationes ejus cum hostibus Reformatorum. Detegamur secundò, quia ob hæreses plurimas, & multiplicem idololatriam est infamis. Tertiò, quia est cauponans verbum Dei, religionem ipsam, Ecclesiastica officia, omnia denique sacra. Unde ipsum veré Simoniacum dixeris. Quarto, quia nullam habet jurisdictionem in Reformatos. Si ipsam excommunicationem per se consideres, inanis est & futilis; tum quia excommunicat fideles propter veram fidem, quam Deus à fidelibus requirit; tum quia ordinis judicialis defectu laborat; tum quia falsa causa nititur: Evangelicis enim hæreses & innumera vitia impingit, contra omnem veritatem; tum quia stulta est ejus formula. Si ipsos excommunicatos spectes, est ipso jure nulla, tum quia nullam habent communionem cum Romana Ecclesia, quomodo ergo potest excommunicare eos, qui non sunt in ejus communione; tum quia Jurisdictionem illam Pontificiam exuerunt; dixit enim ipsis Deus, Exi Populemi Babylone. Papæ tamen hoc fulmen & Anathema exercuerunt nulla ratione habita legis & Evangelii. Vt Innocentius III. anno 1202. qui cohortatur Principes, Electores, ut quoniam ipse excommunicatum primo Otthonem & deinde depositum abjecerit, alium sibi deligant ad Imperium. Gregorius IX. anno 1230. qui tanquam superbus primo anno Pontificatus sui cepit excommunicare, Fridericum Imperatorem, pro causis falsis & frivolis, postposito omni ordine judiciario. Innocentius IV. anno 1249. qui tanto zelo in Imperatorem Fridericum provectus est, ut non modò Christianos Principes illi opponeret: sed etiam misso Nuncio ad Sultanum Ægypti, illum à familiaritate ejus, nisus sit avertere. Vnde ille:
units.tr: For if you consider the person of the excommunicator, the Pope cannot by right excommunicate the Evangelicals, since in the cause of the Reformed he is an incompetent and suspect judge. First, because he is a mortal enemy. The Spanish Inquisition, introduced by order of the Pope, bears witness to this abundantly. So many butcheries in France cry out with full throat. The wars kindled in many kingdoms and provinces prove it. (Speak for me today, dearest fatherland Hungary, which from the very beginning of the Reformation down to these times has been forced to bear this fire kindled by the Pope, and is now compelled to carry it still.) The condemnations published by him against the Reformed make it plain. The hostile acts he has given to kings and princes against the Evangelicals confirm it. His consultations with the enemies of the Reformed demonstrate it. Let us also observe secondly, that because of his many heresies and manifold idolatry he is infamous. Thirdly, because he peddles the Word of God, religion itself, the offices of the Church, and in short all sacred things. Hence you could rightly call him a Simoniac. Fourthly, because he has no jurisdiction over the Reformed. If you consider excommunication itself, it is empty and futile: partly because he excommunicates the faithful on account of the true faith, which God requires of the faithful; partly because it suffers from a lack of judicial order; partly because it rests on a false cause, for he charges the Evangelicals with heresies and countless vices, contrary to all truth; partly because his formula is foolish. If you consider the excommunicated themselves, it is void in law: partly because they have no communion with the Roman Church, so how can he excommunicate those who are not in his communion; partly because they have cast off that Papal jurisdiction, for God said to them, Go out, my people, from Babylon. Yet the Popes have exercised this thunderbolt and anathema without any regard to law or Gospel. Thus Innocent III in the year 1202, who urged the princes and electors, since he had excommunicated Otto first and afterwards deposed him, to choose another for themselves for the Empire. Gregory IX in the year 1230, who, puffed up like a proud man in the first year of his pontificate, began to excommunicate the Emperor Frederick for false and frivolous causes, setting aside every judicial order. Innocent IV in the year 1249, who was carried away with such zeal against the Emperor Frederick that he not only set Christian princes against him, but also, by sending a nuncio to the Sultan of Egypt, strove to turn him away from his friendship. Whence that verse:

units.la: Vae mihi contra quem propria pugnant viscera, Petrus quem petram credideram, mihi mortem & insidias praeparavit: Bonifacius VIII. Leonina mente tyrannizans, magis quàm Papisans, universo orbi metum sui & terrorem incutere moliebatur. Iulius II. in Ludovicum XII. Gallorum Regem de quo Poeta:
units.tr: Woe is me, against whom my own bowels fight; Peter, whom I had believed to be the rock, has prepared death and snares for me. Boniface VIII, ruling with a Leonine mind, more like a tyrant than a pope, strove to strike fear and terror of himself into the whole world. Julius II against Louis XII, King of the French, of whom the poet says:

units.la: Fraude capit totum mercator Iulius orbem, Vendit enim coelos, non habet ipse tamen. Genua cui Patrem, Genetricem Gracia partum Pontus & unda dedit, num bonus esse potest? Fallaces ligures, mendax est Gracia Ponto Nulla fides, in te hac singula IVLE tenes.
units.tr: Julius the merchant takes the whole world by fraud, for he sells heaven, yet does not possess it himself. Can he be good, to whom Genoa gave his father, Greece his mother, and the sea and waves his birth? The Ligurians are deceitful, Greece is a liar, the Pontus has no faith: in you, Julius, all these qualities are held together.

units.la: Qui copias emisit contra eum, ense & clavibus accinctus (nam pictores Paulo ensem, sicut Petro clavem tribuunt, Romani autem Pontifices, & Pauli & Petri successores esse volunt) ad Tyberim profectus, Claves in amnem fertur projecisse, haec inferens: Quandoquidem nihil Petri Claves prodessent, Pauli ensem quem mox eduxerat auxilio futurum. Iuxta illud:
units.tr: He sent forces against him, girded with sword and keys (for painters give a sword to Paul and keys to Peter, and the Roman pontiffs wish to be the successors of both Paul and Peter). He is said to have set out for the Tiber and thrown the keys into the river, saying this: since the keys of Peter had done no good, the sword of Paul, which he had soon drawn, would be of help.

units.la: Hic gladius Pauli nos nunc defendit ab hoste, Quandoquidem Clavis, nil juvat ista Petri.
units.tr: This sword of Paul now defends us from the enemy, since the key of Peter, that thing, avails nothing.

units.la: Bell. tamen de li. 5. de R.P. c. 8. conatur probare Reges & Principes posse per Excommunicationem suis Regnis & ditionibus exui ex 1. Sam. 15. 23. Quia sprevisti verbum Dei, sprevit similiter te, ne sis Rex & ex 2. Reg. 11. 4. Multos Iojadah assumpsit centuriones, Praecepit autem Iojadah Sacerdos Centurionibus illis, ויאמר אליהם & dixit eis finite illam (Athaliam) exire intra ordines, etiam eum, qui sequitur istam morte afficientes gladio, 1. Quia à Samuele dictum Sauli ממלך 2. Quia Iojada Pontifex interfecit Athaliam. ✠. Ad prius, Samuel מצוה mandatum divinum habebat expressum, ut denunciaret Sauli, quid Deus de illo fieri vellet ✠. 11. Poenituit me Saulem constituisse, למלך Regem, כי שב מאחרי quia aversus est à sequendo me. Palpabilis Bellarmini inconsequentia: Deus in mandatis dedit Samueli, ut suo nomine sententiam contra eum denunciaret. Ergo id juris sempiterni Papæ Romani, in quosvis Reges absque mandato divino expresso exercere possunt. Ille accepit mandatum à Deo. Hic nunquam accepit, nec est acceptarus unquam. ℞. Ad Posterius. A summo Pontifice Vet. Test. ad Romanum Papam claudicat consequentia. 2. Absurdum est dicere authoritate Pontificia interfecisse Athaliam. Nam præter Sacerdotium in Iojadah alia ratio etiam fuit, eaque gemina. 1. Quia civis Regni fuit, at contra tyrannos, qui vi aperta Regnum occupant, civi liberum est insurgere. Pontifex autem Romanus, armat & instruit se se contra eos, in quorum Regna nullum jus habet. 2. Quia nulla ratio dari potest, quâ probari posset Athaliam Reginam fuisse legitimam, fuit enim alienigena, alienigenam autem Reginam habere interdictum est, Deut.17.15. שום תשים עליך מלך אשר יבחר יהוה אלהים בו מקרב אחיך תשים עליך מלך לא תוכל לאת עליך איש נכרי אשר לא אחיך הוא
units.tr: Bellarmine, however, in book 5 of De Romano Pontifice, chapter 8, tries to prove that kings and princes can be stripped of their kingdoms and dominions by excommunication, from 1 Sam. 15. 23: Because you have rejected the word of God, he has likewise rejected you, that you should not be king; and from 2 Kings 11. 4: Jehoiada took many centurions, and Jehoiada the priest commanded those centurions, ויאמר אליהם [vayomer aleihem], and said to them: bring her (Athaliah) out between the ranks, and whoever follows her, put to death with the sword. In reply to the first: Samuel had an express divine command to declare to Saul what God wished done with him (1 Sam. 15. 11: I repent that I have made Saul king, למלך [lemelech], since he has turned back from following me [כי שב מאחרי]). This is a palpable inconsequence of Bellarmine: God gave Samuel a command to pronounce sentence against Saul in his name. Therefore, the Roman Pope can exercise this right of perpetual validity against any kings without an express divine command. Samuel received a command from God; the Pope has never received one, nor ever will. To the second: the inference from the Old Testament high priest to the Roman Pope limps. Moreover, it is absurd to say that Jehoiada slew Athaliah by papal authority. For apart from the priesthood, there was another reason in Jehoiada, and that a twofold one. First, because he was a citizen of the kingdom, whereas against tyrants who seize a kingdom by open force, it is lawful for a citizen to rise up. The Roman Pontiff, however, arms and equips himself against those in whose kingdoms he has no right at all. Second, because no reason can be given by which it could be proved that Athaliah was a lawful queen; for she was a foreigner, and it is forbidden to have a foreign queen (Deut. 17. 15: שום תשים עליך מלך אשר יבחר יהוה אלהים בו מקרב אחיך תשים עליך מלך לא תוכל לתת עליך איש נכרי אשר לא אחיך הוא [sum tasim alekha melekh asher yivchar YHWH Elohim bo mikerev acheikha tasim alekha melekh lo tukal latet alekha ish nokhri asher lo acheikha hu]).
